news.title: Map Shows Where Top 2028 Democrats Are Campaigning Ahead of Midterms
news.text: Potential 2028 Democratic presidential candidates like former Vice President Kamala Harris, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg are hitting the campaign trail in the final stretch of the 2026 midterm elections. Harris, who is seen as an early frontrunner in polling, campaigned in Mississippi this week and has planned stops in New Hampshire over the weekend. Ocasio-Cortez attended an event in Maine on Thursday, is in Bakersfield, California, on Friday, and will attend an early-voting rally in North Las Vegas, Nevada, on Saturday, while Buttigieg campaigns in Georgia. The campaign appearances come as Democrats hope to retake control of the House of Representatives and Senate in this year’s elections, as President Donald Trump’s declining approval rating fuels their optimism about a “blue wave” election. Democrats hope appearances by prominent national figures could build enthusiasm among their base, a critical goal in the midterms, when candidates are turning to efforts to motivate voters to head to the polls. But these campaign stops also give potential presidential candidates an opportunity to connect with primary voters ahead of the 2028 Democratic presidential primary and elevate their message and policies. Presidential hopefuls may also be working to build relationships with allies who could deliver important endorsements in the election. Although the first votes will not be cast for more than a year, potential candidates could begin announcing their campaigns soon after the midterms are over, and talk of the presidential primary has already begun. Where Are Potential 2028 Democratic Candidates Campaigning? Candidates are campaigning in several states with competitive races like Michigan and Georgia, but have also notably spent significant time in early voting states like South Carolina, Nevada and New Hampshire. Here is a look at where potential candidates are spending their time ahead of the midterms. Some candidates who have been floated as potential candidates, like Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff and Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, are up for reelection this year and have spent more time in their own states, rather than campaigning for other Democrats. Grant Davis Reeher, professor of political science at Syracuse University, told Newsweek that the hope at this “late stage” is “not to persuade voters but to energize those already inclined to support a candidate and drive them to actually turnout.” “Each is trying to benefit off the other, and potential presidential candidates get the extra benefit of generating goodwill with the other candidate by helping them out,” he said. “That can assist them during the primary season. For the candidate being helped by the presidential hopeful, it can draw more attention to them, and help energize voters to actually turnout.” Newsweek reached out to Harris, Ocasio-Cortez, Newsom, Buttigieg, Kelly and Beshear for comment via email. Kamala Harris Harris has been making campaign stops in places like Mississippi, Nevada and Michigan. She is set to appear in Manchester and Portsmouth, New Hampshire, over the weekend, and is also set to appear in Wisconsin with Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Crowley on Monday, October 26. “Mississippi matters,” Harris said during the rally in Columbus, Mississippi, with Senate candidate Scott Colom. “We’ve got work to do. We’ve got 12 days to make history.” Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez Ocasio-Cortez has spent her time rallying with progressive candidates in key contests like Troy Jackson in Maine’s Senate race, Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan’s Senate race, Angie Nixon in Florida’s Senate race and Randy Villegas in California’s 22nd District. She has also campaigned with some of her colleagues, such as Representative Emilia Sykes in Ohio, and is set to campaign with Representative Steven Horsford in Nevada this weekend. She has also spent time in Western and Upstate New York. Some Democrats have also speculated that she could run for Senate in New York, rather than run for president, in 2028. Gavin Newsom Newsom has traveled to swing states like New Hampshire and North Carolina, but has also toured the South, visiting states like Alabama and South Carolina. Pete Buttigieg Buttigieg, the former Transportation Secretary during the Biden administration, has spent significant time on the campaign trail. This weekend, he is spending time in Atlanta, Georgia, to support Senator Jon Ossoff’s reelection. He wrote in a post to X on Friday, “It's time to get out the vote, Georgia! I hope you'll join Senator Jon Ossoff and me in Atlanta tomorrow afternoon. Together, we can get out the vote for Democrats up and down the ballot in the Peach State.” He has also spent time in New Hampshire and Michigan, where he campaigned with congressional candidate Sean McCann in Kalamazoo. Mark Kelly Senator Kelly of Arizona has been to numerous states including Georgia, Michigan and South Carolina. Most recently, he and other potential candidates appeared at IndyFest in Las Vegas this week, where he said he has not made a decision about whether he will run, reported The Nevada Independent. Andy Beshear Beshear, the governor of Kentucky, was also in attendance at IndyFest and said he did not have an “announcement today” about whether he will join the presidential race, according to The Nevada Independent. He will be spending the next few weeks campaigning in several states including Nevada, New Mexico, Georgia, Ohio, Wisconsin, Iowa, Kansas, and Oklahoma, according to a press release from the Democratic Governors Association. More details on those visits remained unclear. Where Is Donald Trump Campaigning? Democrats aren’t the only ones busy campaigning in the final stretch of the midterms. Trump has held numerous rallies in recent weeks. He rallied in Iowa on Thursday to support Senate candidate Ashley Hinson and gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn, who are both facing competitive races despite the conservative lean of the state. On Friday, he held a rally in Fort Myers, Florida. He is also rallying in Perry, Georgia, on Saturday and Port Huron, Michigan, on Sunday. Next week, he is set to campaign in Corinth, Mississippi, Lubbock and Corpus Christi, Texas, and Chillicothe, Ohio. Democrats’ Chances of Taking House, Senate in Midterms Both the House and Senate are seen as competitive ahead of the midterms. On Friday, the Cook Political Report shifted 19 House races toward Democrats. It now gives Democrats an edge in 220 races and Republicans an advantage in 198 races. Seventeen others are toss-ups. Recent polling has given Democrats an advantage on the generic ballot. These polls can signal the mood of the electorate, but are not always entirely accurate and have overestimated Democrats in some recent cycles. The latest polling data from The New York Times and Siena University, conducted among 3,494 likely voters from October 12 to 19, showed Democrats up 11 points, 52 percent to 41 percent. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 1.9 percentage points. Democrats also led by 11 points among 1,179 “strict” likely voters in the latest poll from YouGov, which surveyed 1,501 registered voters from October 19 to 20. The latest data from Echelon Insights gave Democrats a more modest 5-point lead, 50 percent to 45 percent. It surveyed 1,010 likely voters from October 15 to 19, and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.6 percentage points. The Senate is seen as a tougher lift for Democrats. Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority. If Democrats hold onto every seat they currently hold, including seats in Trump-won Georgia and Michigan, they must flip four seats to win it, as Vice President JD Vance would serve as the tiebreaker in a split chamber. They view GOP-held seats in Maine, which backed Harris by 7 points in 2024, and North Carolina, which Trump carried by 3 points, as top targets. But no other Republican-held seats are up for grabs in states he won by single digits or outright lost in 2024, meaning Democrats have to turn to more conservative turf to win a majority. Polling suggests several double-digit Trump states are going to be competitive. On Friday, RealClearPolitics’ polling average showed Democrats up 1.2 points in Alaska, 3.1 points in Ohio and 1.8 points in Texas. Republicans were up 0.6 points in Iowa and 0.3 points in Kansas. Those races are all considered to be toss-ups by the Cook Political Report. Prediction markets also favor Democrats for both chambers. On Friday, Kalshi gave Democrats a 91.4 percent chance of winning the House and a 67 percent chance in the Senate. Polymarket had Democrats’ chances of a House majority at 92 percent and gave them a 68 percent chance of winning the Senate. Prediction markets allow traders to buy and sell contracts tied to political outcomes and current events, aggregating real‑money wagers into probability estimates. Prices fluctuate as traders react to polling, fundraising, candidate developments and broader political trends. They measure trader sentiment at a given moment but do not always predict the future accurately. Democrats’ 2028 Primary Chances As of Friday, Kalshi gave Ossoff, who has downplayed presidential speculation by saying he is not interested in running, the best chance of winning the presidential nomination at 15 percent, followed by Newsom and Ocasio-Cortez at 13 percent. Harris followed at 7.3 percent, while Buttigieg had a 4.7 percent chance of winning the nomination. Shapiro’s chances stood at 4.5 percent, followed by Beshear at 4.2 percent and Kelly at 3.5 percent. No other candidate had more than a 3 percent chance of winning the nomination. What Have Potential 2028 Candidates Said About Running? Newsom has said he would not run if Harris runs, telling CNN in September, “I wouldn’t run if she ran.” Harris has declined to rule out a potential run. “I might. I am thinking about it,” she told the Reverend Al Sharpton in April after he asked during the National Action Network’s annual convention if she planned to run for president in 2028. Harris noted that she “served for four years being a heartbeat away from the presidency of the United States.” “I spent countless hours in my West Wing office footsteps away from the Oval Office," she said. "I spent countless hours in the Oval Office and the Situation Room. I know what the job is, and I know what it requires.” Ocasio-Cortez addressed presidential speculation in May in a conversation with David Axelrod, a former adviser to former President Barack Obama. "My ambition is to change this country,” she said. “Presidents come and go. Senate, House seats, elected officials come and go. But single-payer healthcare is forever. A living wage is forever, workers' rights are forever, women's rights, all of that, and so anyways...to a finer point to your question is that when you aren't attached, when you haven't been like fantasizing about being this or that since the time you were 7 years old, it is tremendously liberating." Ossoff has said he does not plan to run. “I have zero interest in running for president in 2028, and frankly zero interest in the 2028 fantasy football right now,” he said on MS Now. news.summary: Potential 2028 candidates like Kamala Harris, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and Pete Buttigieg are hitting the campaign trail.

news.title: Robert De Niro ad urges voters to vote early to avoid what Trump might 'pull on Election Day'
news.text: Actor Robert De Niro appeared in a new political ad Thursday encouraging early voting to ensure liberal votes count no matter what "they" pull on Election Day. The ad, shared by the progressive political group Indivisible, was part of a Hands Off Our Vote campaign to encourage efforts to protect the right to vote, which the "Focker-in-Law" actor claimed was threatened by the Trump administration. "Voting is a constitutional right, but you have to see that this administration and the Supreme Court aren’t paying any attention to our constitutional rights," De Niro said in the video. ROBERT DE NIRO GETS EMOTIONAL AS AMY POEHLER PRAISES HIM FOR SPEAKING 'TRUTH TO POWER' AS REGULAR TRUMP CRITIC In the ad, De Niro, a known critic of President Donald Trump, argued it should be "easy" to support any preferred candidate, whether it be a "would-be king who gets us into a disastrous war and corruptly profits from it" or "candidates who won't cut your healthcare and won't protect pedophiles." "There are some powerful people who want to take away that power. This is Robert De Niro, and I’ve got a message for them: No f---ing way. We're fighting them in the courts and standing up to them in the streets," De Niro said. MARK RUFFALO THREATENS TO 'HULK OUT' AT TRUMP, GOP OVER VOTING RIGHTS AT NYC EVENT He encouraged viewers to vote early to take back their power, suggesting that the Trump administration will likely interfere with the voting process. "Whether by mail or in person, you control when, and then, no matter what they pull on Election Day, your vote will already be banked," De Niro said. The White House responded with a scathing comment. "Robert De Niro is a washed up has-been who hasn’t been relevant in 30 years," spokesman Davis Ingle told Fox News Digital. "Now, he just beclowns himself by spewing hate speech and inciting violence against others. "Instead of embarrassing himself every time he speaks, he should immediately seek help to treat his severe and debilitating case of Trump Derangement Syndrome that has completely rotted his peanut-sized brain." Fox News Digital reached out to Indivisible for comment. De Niro's video followed months of Democratic Party members claiming Trump would attempt to "cheat" or rig the midterm elections in his favor. In a video released in August, former Vice President Kamala Harris claimed Trump and the Republicans were "trying to cheat" and that the results for Democrats must be "too big to rig." LIBERALS FLOAT TRUMP WILL TAMPER WITH, CANCEL MIDTERM ELECTIONS Republicans have called out the effort by Democrats to cast doubt on the elections while they refuse to support election security measures like the SAVE Act. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "It is Democrats bending over backwards to prevent voter ID and proof of citizenship for American elections," Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, told Fox News Digital in February. "It is Democrats demanding that nobody ask questions about election security and irregularities. The projection is jaw-dropping."

news.title: California Democratic Primary Poll Shows Voters Favor Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez
news.text:
California voters have identified their early favorites for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination, and Gov. Gavin Newsom is not among the top two, according to a new California Post poll.

When asked whom they would support if the Democratic primary were held today, Golden State voters placed a Democrat from the East Coast at the top of the field.

Newsom, meanwhile, received only lukewarm marks for his performance as governor and finished third in the hypothetical primary matchup.

New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez led the survey with 18% support. Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg followed closely at 17%.

Newsom drew 14% support. Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly was backed by 10% of respondents, while former Vice President Kamala Harris — who previously represented California as a senator and served as the state’s attorney general — placed fifth with 7%.

McLaughlin & Associates conducted the statewide survey among 800 California voters from Oct. 17 through Oct. 20. The poll has a margin of error of 3.4 percentage points, and 419 respondents answered the Democratic primary question.

“Both Newsom and Harris have not locked up the — what would you call — the progressive or the very liberal vote,” McLaughlin said in an interview. “They’ve got stiff competition for it from AOC and from Buttigieg.”

He added that candidates also need to build a strong demographic coalition, noting that minority voters — including Hispanic, Black and Asian voters, as well as women — make up a significant share of the Democratic primary electorate.

Ocasio-Cortez was particularly dominant among self-identified liberal voters. She received support from 25% of those who described themselves as liberal and 41% of those who identified as very liberal.

California voters offered a mixed assessment of Newsom’s job performance: 47% approved, while 50% disapproved. That included 41% who expressed strong disapproval. Independent voters were especially critical, with 62% saying they disapproved of the governor’s performance.

Fifty-six percent of respondents said California was headed in the wrong direction. Economic concerns — including the cost of living, the state budget, taxes, housing and health care — were the dominant reasons for that pessimistic view.

The poll presented voters with a list of figures frequently mentioned as possible 2028 presidential contenders, including Ocasio-Cortez, Buttigieg, Newsom, Kelly and Harris.

NEXT UP: Is Lindsay Clancy Freed? All About the Duxbury Mother Accused of Killing Her 3 Children

The list also included Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro and Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, who each received 3%; New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker, at 2%; former Ambassador Rahm Emanuel, at 1%; and Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, also at 1%. Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, Colorado Gov. Jared Polis and commentator Stephen A. Smith were included as choices but received no support.

Another 23% of respondents remained undecided.

Jeff Jenkins, a provost professor of public policy, political science and law at the University of Southern California, cautioned that it is still extremely early to draw firm conclusions from 2028 presidential polling. With so much likely to change before the election, he said the surveys offer only limited insight at this stage.

“That said, I think it is interesting that Newsom in particular isn’t doing better — because if polls are tracking anything right now, it would be name recognition,” Jenkins said.

“That doesn’t bode well for him. By contrast, I think few see Harris as a serious candidate, so I’m not surprised by her tally,” he added.

The California Post findings are broadly consistent with other recent surveys showing that enthusiasm for potential presidential campaigns by Newsom and Harris may be fading in their home state.

A September survey from the UC Berkeley Citrin Center and POLITICO found that 37% of California Democrats were excited about a Newsom campaign, compared with 28% who said the same about Harris. Those figures marked a notable decline from March, when more than 40% of California voters expressed enthusiasm for each candidate to run.

National polling has produced a somewhat different picture. Three surveys conducted in October showed Harris leading the potential Democratic field with between 20% and 30% support. Newsom ranked second in each poll, attracting roughly 15%.

“They have national name ID, many of these other candidates don’t,” McLaughlin said. 

Both California Democrats have been making the rounds in key primary states to not only campaign for Democrat politicians but also market themselves to a more national audience. Newsom and Harris have openly acknowledged they are considering White House runs.

Most recently, the governor was in New Hampshire, while Harris will reportedly be in Wisconsin and Georgia later this month. 

The Post reached out to offices for both Newsom and Harris for comment.

news.title: Trump Political Org Pours Millions Into Florida District Race After House GOP PAC Slashed Funding
news.text:
President Donald Trump’s political operation planned to spend money in a competitive House race Thursday after Republicans slashed funding in the district. 

The No Going Back PAC, a super PAC backed by MAGA Inc., is pouring more than $25 million into House races, including $6.3 million in Florida’s 25th district where they hope to defeat Democratic Florida Rep. Jared Moskowitz, Punchbowl News first reported. The Congressional Leadership Fund, the top House super PAC, slashed $6 million in planned advertising to oppose Moskowitz and redirected $9 million to defend House seats held by Republicans. (RELATED: Senate Republicans’ Top PAC Dropping $1 Million Into Deep-Red Mississippi)

The super PAC planned to spend $1 million in Washington’s third district, $85,000 in Florida’s 22nd district, $1 million in Florida’s 14th district and $1.2 million in Montana’s first district. 

NEW: buys are starting to trickle in from No Going Back PAC >> $6.3M in #FL25 to target Jared Moskowitz (D) >> $1M in #WA03 to target MGP (D) >> $85K so far in open #FL22 for Casey Askar (R) >> $1M in #FL14 to target Kathy Castor (D) >>$1.2M in open #MT01 for Aaron Flint (R)— Ally Mutnick (@allymutnick) October 22, 2026

Moskowitz is running against former Republican Boca Raton Mayor Scott Singer, who served as mayor for eight years. He campaigned on delivering “common-sense, America First policies” and standing up against “a radical far-left agenda,” according to his campaign website. 

Cook Political Report moved the race from the “Toss Up” column to “Lean Democratic.” Sabato’s Crystal Ball moved the race’s rating in Moskowitz’s favor. 

Republican Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis unveiled a newly drawn congressional map on May 4 that would help Republicans gain four seats. The map intended to benefit Republicans in the 25th district as it no longer covers its former inland Broward County areas.

Former Vice President Kamala Harris won Florida’s 25th district in a 52.1% to 46.8% margin in the 2024 election. Democratic Florida Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz won the district in 2024 by a 54.5% to 45.5% margin.

Moskowitz defeated his further-left opponent Oliver Larkin in the Aug. 18 primary, despite Larkin receiving endorsements from members of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). Candidates backed by the DSA won several of their races against their incumbent challengers throughout the 2026 primary cycle, including 29-year-old Melat Kiros in Colorado’s first district.

Cook Political Report shifted 19 House races in Democrats’ favor, including four Republican-held seats in Arizona, Colorado, Wisconsin and Virginia.

news.title: 'The Simpsons' resurrects Apu after nearly a decade of silence
news.text: Across 38 seasons of "The Simpsons," the Halloween-themed "Treehouse of Horror" episodes have always been a treat of spooky stand-alone storylines. On Sunday, the show surprised viewers with a major resurrection: Apu, the beloved Kwik-E-Mart operator who had not been heard for the better part of a decade, spoke once again in Springfield.He and his wife, Manjula, were back with a meaty plotline — and the voices of actual Indian American actors: Sunil Malhotra, a veteran voice-over artist, and Janina Gavankar ("The Morning Show")."Bringing Apu back feels like a reclamation. It truly IS his homecoming," Malhotra and Gavankar said Sunday in a joint Instagram post.RECENT ENTERTAINMENT NEWS | Glee reboot officially ordered at Disney+ and HuluApu's unheralded return is a remarkable twist to a yearslong discourse about how the character has represented a painful stereotype for some South Asian Americans. After a 2017 documentary by comedian Hari Kondabolu, "The Problem With Apu," the character was largely exiled from the screen.In "The Problem With Apu," Kondabolu, a self-described fan of the Fox show, tried to process his misgivings. He interviewed a slew of celebrities of South Asian origin, including Kal Penn, Utkarsh Ambudkar and Hasan Minhaj, about growing up with the character. They shared memories of being bullied and called "Apu" as an insult. Adding to their view of Apu as just a caricature was that Hank Azaria, a white actor, voiced him.With the full name of Apu Nahasapeemapetilon Jr., he felt like the "forever foreigner, someone who represents Indians in the United States through this sole typology of being a convenience store owner, being a recent immigrant, having this heavy accent, being really limited in this sort of like American identity," says Bhoomi Thakore, an assistant professor of sociology at the University of Connecticut. Thakore notes that Kondabolu's film raised the notion that Apu was the only portrayal of an Indian character most people knew when he debuted in 1990.Azaria stepped away from the role after the documentary, continuing to voice other "Simpsons" characters, as Apu fell silent, seen only in the background. Kondabolu, however, had never called for Apu to be canceled. On Monday, he praised "The Simpsons" for devising "a clever solution to all this" and hiring Malhotra and Gavankar.MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS | 'Widow’s Bay' makes Emmy history while 'The Pitt' underwhelms"I'm also still proud of the public conversation about race and representation my documentary started," he told The Associated Press in an emailed statement. "Finally, I'm hoping this stops all the hatemail in many languages that has been sent my way over the past decade."In a 2018 episode, "The Simpsons" responded to Kondabolu's documentary by having Lisa Simpson bemoan how "something that started decades ago and was applauded and inoffensive is now politically incorrect. ... What can you do?" The camera then panned to a framed photo of Apu. The gag was branded by some as weak for not directly addressing the controversy.In a 2020 New York Times interview, Azaria, who by then hadn't voiced Apu in a few years, announced he would bow out because "it just didn't feel right." Later that year, in response to racial reckoning demonstrations, "The Simpsons" announced it would no longer cast white voice actors as characters of color. The show then recast two Black characters, Carl Carlson and Dr. Julius Hibbert, with Black actors.Kondabolu had not spoken with "The Simpsons" producers about Apu's comeback, he confirmed to the AP, "but they didn't owe me that." And it does sound like Apu is here to stay."We love this character and wanted to bring him back in a smart, Simpsons-y way that allowed him to evolve," executive producer Matt Selman said in a statement. "We're excited by what Sunil has already brought to the role and look forward to seeing more of Apu in the future."A few weeks after "The Simpsons" responded to the documentary, author and producer Amar Shah wrote a series of social media posts and then a Washington Post op-ed on why he felt mostly sentimental toward Apu. When he watched Apu, he thought of his own Indian father hard at work as a convenience store owner and how that shaped his Florida childhood."Apu even now is a character that I wouldn't mind my kids seeing represented because they'll see aspects of themselves and of their own grandparents," says Shah, reflecting on his 2018 piece. "I can totally empathize with someone of South Asian origin having a different POV (point of view) than me but this is my childhood. This is my story."After watching this latest episode, Shah didn't sense any significant difference with Malhotra's performance."Obviously, there's a different voice, tenor, texture and all that. But, the character is always going to be there, his genuine humanity," Shah says. "I think if they had incorporated this change earlier, it would have been a lot better."Apu is being revived amid a climate of rising anti-South Asian and Indian hate. Stop AAPI Hate and other research groups have found online use of racist slurs and threats against South Asians and Indians have jumped in the past few years.Texas Railroad Commission candidate Bo French, a Republican, recently posted a photo of South Asian University of Texas students cheering at a football game and called them "a problem." Just last week, a man was charged with planning a mass shooting at a Hindu temple outside Chicago. Against that backdrop, Shah welcomes the show's careful approach reincarnating the character."It's great to see that the show has evolved in time and now, especially with the discrimination and, really, the targeting of South Asians and Indian Americans as of late — questioning our patriotism, our American identity and even whether we're college football fans," he says.The return also coincides with much more representation of prominent South Asian Americans, such as actor and showrunner Mindy Kaling, and people who have broken barriers in office, like New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and former Vice President Kamala Harris.When Apu first appeared, says University of Virginia associate professor of media studies Shilpa Davé, he was one of the only consistent representations of South Asians on TV.Now, she says, "South Asians have become a part of the landscape from 'Bridgerton' to … 'Never Have I Ever' and there's a plethora of different kinds of representation."
news.summary: On Sunday, the show surprised viewers with a major resurrection: Apu, the beloved Kwik-E-Mart operator who had not been heard for the better part of a decade, spoke once again in Springfield.

news.title: Natasha Lyonne Sparks Backlash Over Controversial Trump Posts as Critics Accuse Her of 'Going Full MAGA'
news.text:
Poker Face star Natasha Lyonne is pushing back against speculation that she supports Donald Trump after a series of posts about the president and Vice President JD Vance sparked confusion among her followers.

Lyonne addressed the backlash on Oct. 21, telling one person who asked whether she was now MAGA, "Not MAGA." 

Her clarification came after two posts the actress shared the previous day prompted questions about her political views.Lyonne Takes Aim at JD Vance, Says She'd "Prefer Trump"The controversy began Oct. 19 after a video from a Republican campaign rally in Hendersonville, N.C., circulated online. 

Vance was speaking when a man interrupted the event by shouting about the Jeffrey Epstein files before being escorted out.

Lyonne reacted to the footage on X, calling Vance a "sketchy m---." In a follow-up post Oct. 20, she wrote, "Sketchy m--- - prefer Trump," while describing Vance's remarks as "even scarier."

She also referenced late author Octavia Butler, calling her a "soothsayer," and described the political climate as "Grimey times." 

Lyonne's apparent preference for Trump over Vance quickly became the focus of questions from followers.Emoji Post About Trump and Elon Musk Fuels MAGA RumorsAnother post added to the confusion.

On Oct. 20, Trump praised Elon Musk for pledging to give one share of SpaceX stock to every child in the United States through the Trump Accounts initiative. 

Trump called Musk his "legendary friend" and said the program was intended to bring the private sector together to invest in children.

Lyonne quote-posted Trump's message without adding an explanation. Instead, she responded with four emojis: a rocket, a saluting face, a sun, and a smiling face with sunglasses.

The post was later deleted, but not before followers questioned whether the response signaled support for Trump and Musk.Actress Clarifies: "Not MAGA" and "Make America Gay Again"As speculation grew, Lyonne addressed the issue more directly. After writing "Not maga," she later posted rainbow and transgender pride flags with the hashtag "#MakeAmericaGayAgain."

She also wrote, "sorry - thought these were just murmurs into the ether - didn't realize it was a whole thing." 

In other replies, Lyonne dismissed the MAGA accusations as "bulls---" and said she planned to delete the posts, while adding that she thought the joke was funny.

The reaction was notable because Lyonne publicly supported Kamala Harris during the 2024 presidential election. In February 2025, she also told The Hollywood Reporter that she was "pretty horrified" by the MAGA movement.Past Airline Incident Resurfaces Amid Social Media StormThe political backlash comes months after Lyonne was involved in a separate controversy aboard a Delta flight.

Page Six reported that around April 7, Lyonne was escorted from a Delta red-eye flight to New York City after allegedly failing to follow crew instructions before takeoff. 

She later referenced missing a scheduled appearance on The Drew Barrymore Show and claimed on X that ICE had detained her during the incident.

The airline incident became another widely discussed moment involving the actress, but her recent political posts have centered the conversation on what she meant by her comments about Trump and Vance.
news.summary: Natasha Lyonne reacted to the controversy that emerged from her social media posts. The posts were targeted at Donald Trump and JD Vance.

news.title: Democrats Will Impeach Trump Again, But It’ll Help His Popularity, Politico Poll Finds
news.text:
Most people think Democrats will impeach President Donald Trump again if they win on November 3, even though the past two impeachments were ineffectual - and more think it’ll increase Trump’s popularity than believe it’ll make him less popular, a new Politico poll reveals.

What’s more, just as many of those planning to vote Democrat on Nov. 3 say their candidates should conceal their plans to impeach Trump - if it’ll help them win - as say they should admit they’ll impeach, even if it hurts their campaigns.

In a national poll of U.S. adults conducted October 16-19, Politico asked a series of questions regarding a potential third impeachment of Trump by Democrats, if they gain control of the House in the midterm elections.

More than two-thirds (69%) of adults said that it’s likely that Democrats will try to impeach Trump if they win the House, including 41% who say it’s “very likely.” That belief is even stronger among those who voted for either Trump (77%) or Democrat Kamala Harris (75%) in the 2024 presidential election. Meanwhile, half (50%) of those who didn’t vote deemed impeachment likely.

Only 18% called it unlikely that a Democrat-majority House would try to impeach Trump, while 13% replied that they “don’t know.”

Ironically, more U.S. adults said Democrats’ third impeachment of Trump would make him more popular (24%) than said it would hurt his popularity (18%). Another 34% said it wouldn’t have an effect, while 24% didn’t know.

The plurality’s belief that another impeachment would boost, not hurt, Trump’s popularity increases with the age, from a virtual tie of 18%-17% among those age 18-24 to a two-to-one advantage (30%-15%) among those 65 and over.

Additionally, only one in four U.S. adults said the impeachments made a difference.

Fully 56% reported that the first and second impeachments “had no real impact on Donald Trump and his agenda,” including 62% of Trump voters and 64% of Harris voters - more than twice the number who said they did have an impact.

Similar percentages of all U.S. adults (24%), Trump voters (26%) and Harris voters (26%) said they think the last two impeachments had an impact.

Notably, winning is more important than honesty for many of those who plan to vote for Democrats in next month’s midterms.

Politico asked whether Democrat candidates should admit to voters that they intend to impeach Trump, even if doing so would hurt their prospects of winning, or hide their plans from the public in order to win.

As it turns out, those advocating deceit ended up in a virtual tie with those who supporting transparency:

“The Democratic candidate should say they plan to impeach Donald Trump, even if that makes it harder to win the election”: 43%“The Democratic candidate should avoid saying they plan to impeach Donald Trump if it helps win the election, even if that means not making their view clear on the matter”: 41%“Don’t know”: 15%

Young Democrat voters (18-24) largely favored openness over deception, 52%-37%. Results were reversed for the oldest (65+), with obfuscation topping honesty, 53%-24%

news.title: If Democrats Aren't Panicking About Minnesota Right Now, They Should Be
news.text:
For all the confidence Democrats are projecting heading into the midterms, they have a lot to worry about.

History alone should give them pause. Midterm polling has a long track record of missing badly, and plenty of races Democrats think they can win because the polls tell them so could easily flip red or stay red. The bigger headache for the Democrat Party, though, sits in the races it assumed were already locked up.

Minnesota should be setting off alarm bells in the Democrat Party right about now.

Despite Minnesota being a reliably blue state, Kamala Harris only carried it by five points in 2024, and she had its own governor, Tim Walz, on the ticket with her. That was supposed to be a home-field advantage.

And that was before the massive fraud scandal blew up in their faces.

On Tuesday, the nonpartisan Cook Political Report shifted the Senate race from Likely Democrat to Lean Democrat. Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, the Democrat nominee, still clings to a narrow edge, leading by four points in a Minnesota Star Tribune poll from earlier this month. That lead falls within the margin of error, which makes it a lead-in-name-only.

But it’s getting even worse for Flanagan.

On Wednesday, NBC News chief data analyst Steve Kornacki went on the Today show and made it quite clear that the GOP can win this election.

"There does seem to be a tide within the state that's working against Democrats," Kornacki said.

He pointed out that Republicans have "been trying for decades" to win that Senate seat, and he didn't need long to explain why the GOP finally likes its odds.

"What they think is working in their favor here is there's a state scandal there about Medicaid fraud," he explained. "The governor, Tim Walz, didn't run for reelection because of it — this is his lieutenant governor."

Steve Kornacki sees tide "working against" Democrat in the Minnesota Senate race “There does seem to be a tide within the state that’s working against Democrats” https://t.co/lJ8GtOE2cK— OSZ (@OpenSourceZone) October 22, 2026

Kornacki is hardly a GOP cheerleader, which makes his read all the more delicious. When the guy at the big board on a network morning show starts talking about a tide turning against Democrats in Minnesota, the one state in the union that never voted for Ronald Reagan, the party has a real problem on its hands.

ICYMI: Still Think Talarico Will Flip Texas? You Might Want to Read This.

That problem is Flanagan's own record. Republican Michele Tafoya has hammered her for failing to stop a sprawling fraud and money laundering scheme that prosecutors believe drained at least $9 billion from the state. Let’s not forget, the fallout got bad enough that Walz abandoned his reelection bid earlier this year, as scrutiny of his handling of the mess mounted. He knew it would kill his chances and risk flipping the governorship to the GOP. Now, Flanagan, who served as his second in command the entire time, is the party’s nominee for the U.S. Senate, and that’s giving Tafoya a real shot.

And trust me, Tafoya is making sure voters don’t forget that Flanagan was part of the problem. When Flanagan turned the conversation to lost access to programs during a debate last week, Tafoya pounced.

"Listen, it is rich to hear my opponent talk about lost access to programs when under her watch, as second in command of this state, Minnesota saw billions and billions and billions of fraud dollars walk out the door to fraudsters while Medicaid was gutted," Tafoya said.

Flanagan's answer was hardly a profile in courage.

"The governor said that more should have been done and more should have been done sooner, and I agree with him," Flanagan said in response. "But I supported the independent office of inspector general. I also supported harsher penalties."

That’s… a terrible defense.

She concedes the response came too late, then points to an inspector general's office and some tougher penalties, as if they make up for billions in stolen taxpayer money. Voters who watched that cash vanish on her watch won't find a list of things she supported after the damage was done to be impressive. They want to know why it wasn’t caught in the first place, and the signs have long pointed to Democrat leaders simply letting it happen because they risked losing support from the Somali community.

Democrats can keep projecting confidence all they want, but if Minnesota is competitive this year, trust me, they’ve got a lot of problems.

news.title: Abdul El-Sayed's Appeal to Black Voters Jumped on By Conservatives
news.text: Several conservative accounts on X have criticized Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed as "pandering" to Black voters after he was seen ordering fried chicken while discussing his efforts to build trust with the voting bloc. In an interview with The Root, a Black-oriented online magazine, the issue of building trust with Black voters was discussed with El-Sayed as he runs a crucial Senate campaign against Republican Mike Rogers. El-Sayed's campaign has attempted to shore up support among Black voters who make up roughly 11 to 12 percent of Michigan’s electorate, following struggles evident during the Democratic primary. Some critics online said that his order of fried chicken invoked racial stereotypes. Conservatives Call His Interview A 'Joke' Eric Daugherty, a prominent pro-Trump media personality was among those who highlighted the interview. “To appeal to black voters in Michigan, Abdul El Sayed orders fried chicken,” Daugherty wrote on X, adding: “What a freaking JOKE.” Conservative radio host and political commentator Jesse Kelly characterized the order as “pandering to Black people.” "End Wokeness," another prominent conservative X account, also highlighted the choice of order. “All he needed was some grape drank and some watermelon and he would have completed the trifecta of ‘black food,’ " wrote Zeke Arkham, who describes himself as a conservatarian on X, where he has over half a million followers. If elected, El-Sayed would become the first Muslim U.S. senator. While some called the food order and attempt to target Black voters, El-Sayed’s order was also among several menu items containing halal meat, which means permissible under Islamic law, according to the restaurant’s online menu. Newsweek contacted El-Sayed’s campaign for comment via email on Wednesday. Michigan's Importance in the Midterms The Michigan race is central to Democrats' hopes to take control of the upper chamber in the midterms. Democrats need to defend all of their currently held seats, including in Michigan, and flip four GOP-held seats to take the majority. The state has not elected a Republican to Senate since 1994. Cook Political Report rates the contest as a toss-up and Sabato's Crystal Ball rates it "Likely Democratic." Primary Data Pointed to Challenges In Key Bloc Both July polling and the August primary results pointed to weaknesses in El-Sayed’s support among Black voters. Polling leading up to Michigan’s Democratic primary suggested Representative Haley Stevens, who was competing against El-Sayed in that contest, held an advantage among Black voters overall, especially those older than 55, while El-Sayed performed better among younger and college-educated voters across racial groups. Stevens led El-Sayed by eight percentage points in districts where more than 15 percent of the population was Black, according to primary results reported by The Hill, which also noted that July polling showed just 21 percent of Black voters supported El-Sayed while 67 percent favored Stevens. One Michigan political organizer attributed the divide in support to generational and ideological differences among Black voters. Kermit Williams, political director of the Oakland Forward Action Fund, told Capital B News that older Black voters in Michigan tended to favor Stevens’ emphasis on experience, while younger, more progressive Black voters were more receptive to former public health official El-Sayed’s push for sweeping change. “I think that older and more established Black voters believe in incremental change,” Williams told the outlet. “And when you start talking about younger Black voters, they want to see a whole new system. I think that El-Sayed has kind of tapped into that energy.” Campaign’s Outsider Strategy Drew Concerns Democratic strategists have also suggested that El-Sayed’s anti-establishment message—a key part of his outsider campaign to challenge the Democratic establishment—sometimes put him at odds with Black political institutions. “Attacks on the Democratic establishment in places like Detroit are attacks on Black leaders,” Jamal Simmons, former communications director for Vice President Kamala Harris, told The Hill. Basil Smikle, a political strategist and policy advisor for over two decades, told the outlet, “He ran against the Democratic Party and while flawed, it was a vehicle through which African American voters and their representatives found political and economic paths to power.” Some reporting has also suggested that some viewed El-Sayed’s primary outreach efforts as either too limited or too late. The American Prospect reported that, during a post-primary roundtable with Black mayors and other Michigan elected officials, several participants told El-Sayed they had not seen enough of him on the campaign trail, with some saying he had not campaigned in their communities—a characterization he disputed. “I’ll just tell you, through the course of the primary, I’ve actually been to every one of your cities,” El-Sayed said, according to the outlet, which reported that he acknowledged he may not have campaigned directly with each of them but had sought the support of their constituents. El-Sayed has also faced questions over his involvement in the 2024 “uncommitted” movement, which urged Democrats to register their opposition to the Biden administration’s response to the war in Gaza by voting uncommitted in the presidential primary. More than 100,000 Michigan Democrats voted this way, and interviews conducted by CNN with Black voters and party leaders indicated that some remained wary of El-Sayed because of his role in that movement. More Recent Polling Offers Mixed Signs Polling ahead of the November election paints a more encouraging picture for El-Sayed than the primary data, although it still points to some potential weakness among Black voters. A September Washington Post-Schar School poll found that 83 percent of Black voters wanted Democrats to control the Senate, but only 67 percent intended to vote for El-Sayed, hinting at a candidate-specific gap inside an otherwise strongly reliable Democratic constituency. That poll surveyed 803 likely Michigan voters from September 10 to September 14 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.9 percentage points. Crosstabs from a Fox News poll conducted September 24 to September 28 indicated that around 77 percent of likely Black voters supported El-Sayed. In 2024, Vice President Kamala Harris received 87 percent of the Black vote in the state, according to CNN exit numbers. Harris campaigned alongside El-Sayed last month in Detroit, after endorsing him following his August primary win. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: John Fitzpatrick and Geoffrey Rowland.
news.summary: Primary results showed weaknesses for El-Sayed among Black voters, though recent polls offer a more encouraging, mixed picture.

news.title: Donald Trump Calls LeBron James 'A Total Disgrace' Over National Anthem Actions at 76ers Game
news.text: LeBron James' dormant feud with Donald Trump was reignited during his first game with the Philadelphia 76ers.The president of the United States slammed the athlete online during the team's season opener on Tuesday, 20 October. The video ended with the text 'Hate Takes Us Back', after Trump was recorded saying, 'Of course I hate these people and let's all hate these people because maybe hate is what we needed,' although the context of the president's statement was unclear.Trump Blasts LeBron James Amid Controversy Over Transgender AthletesTrump maintained the stance that transgender women do not have a place in women's sports. The issue became a hot topic in 2022 after Lia Thomas, a transgender swimmer, competed at the NCAA Women's Swimming and Diving Championships. Thomas, who previously competed on the men's team, tied for fifth place with Riley Gaines, a cisgender woman, in the 200-yard freestyle.The issue was brought up again after Sophie Cunningham recently made a statement expressing that women's spaces and sports should be protected from transgender participation.Trump criticised transgender athletes who competed in women's sports before directing the spotlight to James in 2022. The president declared that he would be the greatest women's basketball coach in history and joked that he would ask James whether he had 'any desire to be a woman' so that he could play on his hypothetical team.

news.title: First-Term Trump Lawyer Makes Damning Prediction About $10B Lawsuit
news.text:
Donald Trump won’t play ball in his $10 billion lawsuit, a former lawyer for the president has claimed. 

First-term White House attorney Ty Cobb appeared on CNN’s OutFront on Thursday and said there was no way the 80-year-old would sit through the entire deposition the BBC called for. 

The British media titan is fighting back against the suit Trump brought against it over an episode of its show Panorama. On Thursday, the judge backed the corporation and ordered him to sit and be deposed by its lawyers. 

“So, Trump wants $10 billion. Now he’s being ordered to answer questions under oath,” host Erin Burnett said. “How much has this backfired on him?”

“Oh, it’s backfired,” Cobb said. “Trump, as we know, has sued multiple media outlets about stories that he didn’t like even though the reporting was truthful. Many of those outlets—domestic-owned outlets—overpaid Trump to try to curry favor with him.”

U.S. media giants ABC and CBS both settled with the president after they were sued by him. 

ABC agreed to pay Trump $16 million to settle a case after anchor George Stephanopoulos said the president had been “found liable for rape” in E. Jean Carroll’s civil case when the jury found him liable for sexual assault. CBS’s parent company, Paramount, also agreed to pay $16 million to settle Donald Trump’s lawsuit after he complained that a 60 Minutes interview with Kamala Harris was deceptively edited. The money was designated for Trump’s future presidential library.

“The BBC’s lawyers are doing the right thing,” Cobb continued. “They’re defending, and they’re not going away. Trump has dragged it out. He’s the plaintiff in the case. He’s the one that invented these claims.” 

He sued the BBC over its coverage of the 2024 election after it edited together clips his team says make it seem like he encouraged violence at the Capitol on January 6. Only two months of discovery remain in the case, and the broadcaster’s lawyers say they “still haven’t been able to depose the plaintiff.”

Trump skipped a seven-hour deposition scheduled for October 16, citing a “matter of national importance.” However, he did have time that day to attend a rally in Dalton, Georgia.

He now must sit for a deposition on December 11 or face sanctions and the possibility that the case will be thrown out. 

“He contests the way that they edited actual excerpts of his Jan. 6 exhortation for an insurrection. And he didn’t like the way they pieced it together. So he complained about it, hoping they would cave and pay him off, but they didn’t. And they’re trying to get his deposition, which they’re entitled to, or the case will be dismissed,” Cobb added. 

The case also includes a BBC subpoena for membership records from Trump’s Mar-a-Lago resort. U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett has supported it, and Cobb says it all relates to the impact on Trump’s reputation. 

“So, it’s not really clear what that will reveal other than it will go somewhat to how much was Trump really damaged?” he said. And that’s a very narrow subset of what will be explored in the deposition. 

“You know, they can go into anything that affects Trump’s reputation, the reputation of his multiple bankruptcies, his business acumen. They will be able to go into all the personal issues from the 34 felonies to the Epstein files to the selling of pardons at this stage of the game.

“So, this will be wide-ranging, which is why Trump will never sit for it. He’s likely to refuse to go. If he does go, he’ll walk out in the middle, and the case will ultimately get dismissed unless the plaintiffs are entitled to and receive his full testimony.”

Cobb left Trump’s White House legal team in May 2018 with reports saying he disagreed with how aggressively Trump should fight Robert Mueller’s Russia investigation.

The Daily Beast has contacted the White House for comment.

news.title: Is the Role of Money in Politics Overstated?
news.text:
The old saw that money is the mother’s milk of politics is a bipartisan truism universally recognized on both sides of the aisle. Anyone who wants to become a political princess or prince must be able to play the pauper, incessantly shaking the tin can in desperate appeals for the cash that, would-be leaders proclaim, spells the difference between victory and defeat.

This year’s crop of candidates appear to have mastered the role of beggar. AdImpact projects that $11.6 billion will be spent on political ads this cycle, the most ever for a midterm election and even more than the 2024 presidential election. Super PACs and other interest groups have nearly doubled their spending since the 2022 midterms, while billionaires including Elon Musk and Michael Bloomberg have made headlines for their gargantuan contributions.

A RealClearInvestigations analysis of campaign spending in federal races since 2012, however, challenges the bedrock assumption that superior fundraising buys victory. Although a majority of the candidates who raised the most money won their races, most of them likely would have won anyway thanks to the power of incumbency or the safety secured by gerrymandering. In the relatively small number of truly competitive races, the advantage of a bigger war chest was almost negligible.

Political scientists have found that politicians only need a certain threshold of money to run a viable campaign. After that, other factors – the candidate’s incumbency and charisma, the prevailing political winds and the state of the economy – are more important. 

“To the extent people believe it’s an automatic, ‘If you’ve got more money you’re gonna win,’ that is clearly not true,” said Bradley Smith, founder of the Institute for Free Speech (IFS) and former chairman of the Federal Election Commission. “What spending does is it allows you to get your message out to voters, and from there you’ve got to have an attractive message or personality or total political package to win.”

Election experts told RCI the overemphasis on fundraising is affecting the nation’s politics. It leads candidates to spend a lot of time seeking money to pay for often misleading attack ads, instead of sharpening their message. It leads media outlets to devote resources to covering the fundraising instead of the issues. And it instills cynicism among voters: Three out of four Americans agree there is too much money in politics, and almost half believe that wealthy people or organizations can outright “buy” election victories.

Cause or effect?

FEC filings show that since 2012, the candidate who raised the most money won nine out of 10 federal elections. RCI found that wide fundraising gaps had a strong statistical correlation with landslide victories. 

However, those statistics include scores of races where the outcome was all but predetermined. Rep. Nancy Pelosi outraised her opponent $10.2 million to $207,000 in 2024 and won easily – but her victory was hardly dependent on fundraising. There was little chance her San Francisco district – where Democrats outnumber Republicans more than five to one – would ever elect a Republican. She won with 80% of the vote, which is not rare in our highly gerrymandered country. Research shows that more than 90% of House incumbents like Pelosi who have stood for re-election, and 86% of incumbent U.S. senators, have won their races since the mid-1960s.

That makes it difficult to decipher whether money actually causes election victories. Candidates with the political prowess to win a seat in Congress are usually the ones donors are excited to give to. “Political scientists have been skeptical of the causal impact of money, because those who raise the most money are often expected to be the most likely to win. It’s really hard to untangle how much of it is material,” said Dr. Danielle Thomsen, professor of political science at the University of California, Irvine, and author of “The Money Signal: How Fundraising Matters in American Politics.”

The picture changes significantly when the focus is narrowed to competitive races – those where the victor wins by 10% or less. RCI’s analysis found that large fundraising gaps only had a weak correlation with the candidate’s margin of victory. Supporters of both Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris, for example, vastly outspent those of Donald Trump in their losing 2016 and 2024 campaigns, respectively. But because spending statistically has less impact in tight races, Trump was still able to win the presidency.

In Michigan’s 2024 Senate race, Elissa Slotkin and PACs supporting her outspent Mike Rogers $91 million to $44 million. She barely eked out a victory. In Pennsylvania’s 2024 Senate race, incumbent Bob Casey outraised his challenger $58 million to $36 million but still lost to Dave McCormick.

Overall, there were 555 competitive federal elections from 2012 to 2025. The top fundraiser only won 63% of them. 

“Candidates are mindful of being seriously outspent by their competitors. But at some point, when both candidates spend so much, races are just saturated with information, and spending an additional ‘x’ number of dollars isn’t likely to yield the same rewards,” Thomsen said.

Data can also be skewed by panic spending. IFS’s Smith said that incumbents who realize they are likely to lose will spend extreme amounts of money in a last-gasp effort to recapture popularity. Rarely does the infusion do much to offset whatever the nation’s prevailing sentiment toward Democrats and Republicans happens to be that year.

“If you’re an incumbent, you’ve already got your name known. Spending doesn’t do as much for you as it does for a challenger,” said Smith. “I don’t think that spending more money actually causes candidates to lose, but it’s indicative that the candidate is likely to lose. The candidate’s losing, and they don’t know what else to do besides spend money.” 

Early money matters

The time and place where campaign fundraising does make a notable difference is early in the primary cycle. Fundraising success tells donors and voters that a candidate has the support needed to win a general election. Since 2012, the top fundraiser has won 80% of primaries, not including uncontested races.

Thomsen’s research found that primary voters often view a candidate more favorably simply because they raised lots of money. She gave politically engaged voters a list of fictional candidates and found those who raised the most money were more likely to attract votes, regardless of the candidates’ political views or platform.

“Early money matters in all of these ways long before the primary election in shaping how candidates are perceived, which competitors are seen as formidable, and which candidates are covered by journalists,” Thomsen said.

Thomsen found the average primary winner in the 1980s and 1990s raised roughly $100,000 during their first three months after announcing their candidacy, adjusted for inflation. Today, it’s closer to $400,000. That’s partly why winners like New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and even President Trump, who won elections despite huge fundraising disadvantages, are becoming increasingly rare exceptions to the norm. It’s harder than ever to pull off a victory without early donor support.

“Imagine you had a really good idea for a soft drink,” said Smith. “But if you want to go out and compete with Coke and Pepsi, you’ve got to go on ‘Shark Tank’ and get somebody to give you some real money. You can’t just do a public offering and hope people will buy stock in your company that they never heard of. You need that champion. Politics can be the same.”

While most incumbents do not need hordes of cash to win re-election, money empowers them in other ways, and they often end up being some of the top fundraisers. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York could likely win reelection this year without spending a single penny, yet she has outraised every House candidate in the country.

Candidates in safe seats still need to fundraise as a deterrent to potential challengers, both Smith and Thomsen said. Ocasio-Cortez’s seat is completely safe in part because her challenger, Diamant Hysenaj, has no political experience and little name recognition. If Ocasio-Cortez’s funds were depleted, perhaps a Republican or primary opponent would have made a more serious attempt to unseat the popular progressive.

“If a challenger sees that you’re not raising any money, and you’re just assuming you’re gonna win reelection, somebody might say, ‘I think that candidate actually has some vulnerability,’” said Smith. “But if you’ve got a huge war chest, that challenger might go, ‘There’s no way I’m gonna beat that incumbent,’ and they don’t even try.”

Well-known candidates also have the easiest time currying donations, and their committees often serve as a fundraising nexus for their entire party. Rep. Brett Guthrie, running for a safe seat in Kentucky in 2024, transferred the majority of his funds to the National Republican Congressional Committee. It was then disbursed to candidates with less name recognition who may have struggled to fundraise on their own.

Incumbents “have longevity, seniority, and a long list of donors, so it’s easier for them to raise money,” Smith said. “So the party presses them, ‘You need to raise money and then give it to other candidates running for the House, because you want to be the majority, don’t you?’”

Unsurprisingly, incumbents rarely acknowledge the fact that money is rarely crucial for them to retain their seat. In an Aug. 31 email blast, Ocasio-Cortez told Democrats she needs their money to “re-elect AOC, defeat our Republican opponent, and show the world what we can do.” In a tacit acknowledgment of her surplus, she gave $1 million to support Abdul El-Sayed’s U.S. Senate run in Michigan. 

Likewise, Vice President JD Vance emailed supporters to let them know “The Democrats are pouring everything they have into stopping” House Speaker Mike Johnson from winning reelection. Johnson’s top challenger has raised only $1.2 million and has virtually no chance of victory, but such messaging is more effective than asking donors to give Johnson money so he can transfer it to other committees and PACs.

Even though money is not determinative in many races, grassroots fundraising continues to grow because writing a check is an easy way for average citizens to feel they are participating in democracy. Yet most donors already know their money is unlikely to sway the race. A 2017 study by the Bipartisan Policy Center found that “overwhelmingly donors are not giving because they think the race is close or they think they could affect the outcome.” Instead, most donors felt it was their “civic duty” to donate, and nearly all said they were “advancing the common good.”

Mega-donors and dark money

More recently, the rise of dark money groups has added more fuel to the fundraising fire. These organizations are legally unaffiliated with candidates and do not disclose the sources of their funding, which are widely believed to come from wealthy donors. These groups spent a record $1.9 billion in 2024, and the Brennan Center for Justice predicts the record will be broken again in 2026.

Political scientists say while there is no evidence that this money influences election outcomes any more than other contributions, its impact may be more corrosive. It highlights the motivations of rich donors who, presumably, are more aware of the limits of their large checks in affecting outcomes, raising questions about whether they are trying to buy access to leaders. In addition, dark money groups often use their funds to run attack ads, which can be misleading, deepening cynicism. 

There are various reasons donors may hide their identities, including protecting their social and business prospects. 

Of course, this year’s largest donor is not secret. Elon Musk gave $366 million to Republican candidates, the largest political donation in U.S. history. The Brennan Center writes, “We have not had a major election where one party’s spending so dwarfs the other’s in at least a half century, likely since the 1972 election that brought us Watergate.”

Yet Democrats are still projected to win control of both chambers of Congress as of Oct. 14, and to win the Texas Senate race, where Musk has concentrated most of his spending. If Democrats do walk out of Election Day with a sweeping victory, it could serve as further evidence that no amount of spending can mitigate factors like the president’s low job approval rating.
news.summary: The old saw that money is the mother's milk of politics is a bipartisan truism universally recognized on both sides of the aisle.
news.author: Jeremy Portnoy,RealClearInvestigations

news.title: Republican 'Muslim Brotherhood' attacks on Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan seek to exploit Democratic fault lines
news.text:
Republican US Senate candidate Mike Rogers and allies including President Donald Trump are escalating their efforts to tie Democratic rival Abdul El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood less than two weeks before the Nov 3 midterms, with Trump falsely branding him a “jihadist.”

Pollsters and political strategists ​say the approach is aimed at dissuading Jewish and Black voters in the Detroit area who backed El-Sayed’s primary opponent, Haley Stevens, from getting behind the Democratic nominee in the closing days ‌of the Senate campaign in Michigan.

“It gives them even more reason to pause and not vote for El-Sayed,” said Dennis Darnoi, a Republican political consultant.

“If Democratic voters aren’t casting ballots for El-Sayed in what is the biggest population area here, then that is a net benefit to Mike Rogers’ campaign.”

El-Sayed and Rogers are vying for the seat held by retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters in a race that could determine whether Democrats gain the four Senate seats needed to take control of the chamber in next month’s election.

Republicans currently have a 53-47 ​seat majority, which would be harder to overturn if El-Sayed loses.

The Democrat has built a small lead in opinion polls by focusing his campaign on affordability, healthcare and getting money out of politics.

Rogers has ​sought to undermine the Democrat’s support among Jewish voters by pointing to El-Sayed’s criticism of Israel’s offensive in Gaza and asserting that El-Sayed has longstanding family ties to the Muslim ⁠Brotherhood.

Strategists said homing in on the Muslim Brotherhood also aims to hurt El-Sayed by exploiting economic tensions between Black voters and Michigan’s large Arab-American community.

Rogers has pointed ​to old social media posts by El-Sayed’s half sister saying their mother was involved with the organisation in the 1970s.

El-Sayed has disavowed the Muslim Brotherhood, denied any connection with the group and has said that he was not raised by his ​mother. His parents divorced when he was three years old, and he was raised by his father and step-mother.

Asked about Rogers’ strategy, campaign spokesperson Alyssa Brouillet said El-Sayed’s “extremist positions” on issues ranging from prisons to the Muslim Brotherhood were alienating Michiganders.

El-Sayed campaign spokesperson Roxie Richner said Rogers is trying to distract from the economic effects of Trump’s agenda, adding in a statement: “Independent fact checkers have repeatedly debunked Mike’s lies, but their campaign continues to use bad faith attacks on Abdul’s faith and family.”

‘Proud to be an American’

Rogers hit the Muslim Brotherhood message ​hard during this week’s televised debate, questioning the Democrat’s loyalty to the US.

“If you are going to go to the United States Senate, we need to know: are you for America or are you for these terrorist groups overseas?” Rogers asked.

El-Sayed, ​a son of Egyptian immigrants who would be the first Muslim to be elected to the US Senate if he wins, responded by calling the question shameful.

“It’s actually quite beneath you, Mike,” he replied. “I am proud of America. I’m proud to be ‌an American. I’m ⁠proud of our Constitution that guarantees all of us the right to pray as we choose to pray.”

Rogers, a former congressman, US Army officer and FBI agent, later appealed directly to Democrats who voted for Stevens, saying they “have a home” with him if they were worried that El-Sayed was too “extreme”.

Michigan Senate race a ‘toss-up’

It is unclear if the Republican strategy is paying off.

The race is rated a toss-up by independent political analysts, with polls showing El-Sayed with an average lead of 2.6 percentage points, according to the website RealClearPolling.com.

El-Sayed has campaigned recently with prominent Black political figures such as Senator Raphael Warnock of Georgia, Representative Ayanna Pressley of Massachusetts and 2024 Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris. Former president Barack Obama, who ​has endorsed El-Sayed, is due to campaign with him ​on Saturday.

Michigan Democratic Party Black Caucus Chair Keith Williams, ⁠who backed Stevens in Michigan’s Democratic primary contest and is now working to rally support for El-Sayed, acknowledged that tensions between the Black and Arab American communities are an issue for the candidate.

“We have to work through our differences,” Williams told Reuters.

“At the end of the day, this election is bigger than our differences because we cannot have a senator ​going to Washington and supporting Donald Trump’s policies.”

Some strategists say the attacks may have come too late to reshape the race and risk backfiring if voters view ​them as anti-Muslim.

“I don’t know what ⁠this does for them,” said Jim Zogby, a longtime pollster and co-founder of the Arab American Institute, a nonprofit that advocates for the Arab American community.

“There are people who think Haitians eat cats and dogs and think anybody with an Arabic name is either a terrorist or a member of the Muslim Brotherhood. But that’s a much smaller group of people — and it’s already a Republican group of people.”

Overwhelming support from Black voters

A September Emerson College poll showed support for El-Sayed at 81 per cent among Black ⁠voters, who make ​up about a quarter of Michigan Democrats.

“There was no sign there in mid-September of erosion of Black support for El-Sayed. I would not ​suspect that the number would have changed much over the last month,” said Matt Taglia, senior director of Emerson College Polling.

Democrat Jocelyn Benson, who is running for Michigan governor, scored 4 percentage points higher in the same poll, while Harris drew 86pc of the Black vote in 2024.

Michigan pollster Steve Mitchell said ​weaker support among Black and Jewish voters could cost El-Sayed as many as 20,000 votes. Rogers lost his 2024 Senate bid to Democrat Elissa Slotkin by a similar margin.

news.title: Trump asserts his right to seek third presidential term
news.text:
WASHINGTON, October 23. /TASS/. Donald Trump said he has the right to run for a third term as US president because the 2020 election he lost to Joe Biden was allegedly fraudulent.

"I think I have the right to run again because they cheated. They rigged the election," he said, addressing a GOP midterm rally in Iowa.

However, the US leader acknowledged that he may be barred by law from running again. "I'm not 100% sure, but I think the law says that I'm not allowed to run again. It says something to the effect that under no circumstances and for any reason will you even consider thinking about running for president," Trump noted.

By law, Trump’s second term as president is scheduled to end in January 2029. The 22nd Amendment to the US Constitution, adopted in 1951, limits a president’s tenure to two terms. Nevertheless, the current US leader has repeatedly raised the possibility of seeking re-election for a third term. Steve Bannon, the president’s former key political strategist, also argued last fall that Trump should serve as president again.

Trump won the election for the second time in November 2024 when he defeated Democratic Party candidate Kamala Harris. He previously led the US administration from 2017 to 2021.
news.summary: The US president still acknowledged that he may be barred by law from running again

news.title: Retired Washington Post, Boston Globe editor discusses journalism career, challenges of the field
news.text:
Two media personalities recently made their way to Elmer’s Community Center in Ashfield for a discussion on the national media landscape, along with the continued attacks against journalists by the federal government.

Indira Lakshmanan, host of NPR’s Here & Now, moderated a discussion with former editor of The Washington Post and The Boston Globe, Marty Baron. The Oct. 15 event, organized by the New England First Amendment Coalition (NEFAC), focused on Baron’s career, issues that newsrooms are currently facing, and what the First Amendment really means (and what it doesn’t mean).

Baron said he can trace the environment of distrust surrounding journalists back to President Donald Trump’s first election in 2016. Similarly, Lakshmanan mentioned that Trump called journalists the enemy of the people, with Baron once again saying his famous line: “We’re not at war with the administration, we’re at work.”

“This is not just about freedom of the press. … It’s about freedom of expression,” Baron said. “Aspiring authoritarians go after the press first because we are the ones who have the capacity and responsibility of holding these institutions and individuals accountable.”

Lakshmanan asked Baron why he thinks many business executives have “basically completely given in” to the Trump administration during his second term, versus his first term where many business owners (particularly Amazon and Washington Post owner Jeff Bezos) butted heads with the president.

Baron described Bezos as “a really great owner” while he was at The Washington Post, but shared that Amazon was passed over for a major contract by the federal government, which Baron links back to the newspaper’s coverage of Trump.

He added that after the storming of the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, “everybody thought, ‘This guy is never coming back.'” Then, when Trump was the Republican nominee in 2024, Baron said Bezos saw a real threat to the financial future of Amazon. To make amends with then-candidate Trump, Bezos killed an endorsement that the staff of The Washington Post had written for Vice President Kamala Harris for the 2024 presidential election.

This led to several thousand people canceling their subscriptions, which Baron said didn’t hurt Bezos, but instead hurt the journalists working at the publication.

“You’re not hurting Jeff Bezos at all,” Baron said about people canceling Washington Post subscriptions. “Cancel your Amazon Prime subscription if you want to hurt Jeff Bezos.”

Outside of the endorsement, Baron said his former colleagues on the news side of The Washington Post tell him that Bezos hasn’t interfered with news reporting. He added that the job of journalists should be to give people the facts, regardless of what those facts say.

“If we’re holding people accountable, it should be everyone,” Baron said, adding that he would cover a Republican and Democrat in scandal the same way. 

With public trust in major media corporations thoroughly eroded, Baron said journalists need to be more transparent than ever, and show the public the process that newsrooms use. This could include linking to certain documents received through Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests, showing the data that certain conclusions were drawn from or showing the entirety of a video instead of a selected sample.

“We know today that many folks don’t trust us, and so we have to lay out the evidence. … The message to the public should be, ‘Check out our work,'” Baron said. “You have the right, and we’re giving you the opportunity to check out our work.”

He said the news organizations that often garner the most trust are local news organizations. However, those local organizations are disappearing at an astonishing rate, leaving news deserts where one or no publications exist.

Where news deserts exist, “corruption does seem to flourish” as no one is there being the watchful eye on government officials, according to Baron. He said local outlets are providing real value to the communities they serve, and that if he had the model on how to keep local publications alive, “I’d be selling it.”

One of the bigger threats to journalism, Baron said, is the rise of artificial intelligence, specifically chatbots such as Claude, Google Gemini and ChatGPT, as these chatbots don’t always verify the information that they’re sharing. He said if he operated as a journalist in the same way chatbots operate, “You would suggest alternatively that I should be fired.”

Baron added that local news organizations need to have direct communication with their audience to build back that trust. While this seems like a gargantuan task, Baron said he is reminded of a quote from Bernard Lown, a Lithuanian-American cardiologist who gave an acceptance speech for a Nobel Prize on behalf of the International Physicians for the Prevention of Nuclear War in 1985.

“Only those who can see the invisible can do the impossible,” Baron said, quoting Lown.
