news.title: Kamala Harris Rallies Mississippi Voters Behind Scott Colom in Senate Race
news.text:
COLUMBUS, Miss.—Former Vice President Kamala Harris stumped for Mississippi U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom at his hometown high school on Oct. 22.

The Democrat and district attorney for the 16th Judicial District of Mississippi has gained ground on his Republican opponent, incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-Miss.), in the Magnolia State as the clock ticks closer to Nov. 3.

Colom’s rise in the Senate race prompted the Cook Political Report to switch the contest from a “Solid Republican” to a “Likely Republican” win as the Senate Majority PAC funneled $1.2 million on an advertisement to boost his campaign.

“I have traveled here because indeed Mississippi matters,” Harris said to an auditorium of approximately 1,000 people.

The former Democratic nominee for president told the crowd that she understands people have been going through a “range of emotions, from anger to … sadness to depression” in Trump’s second term and urged the crowd to “turn that anger into action.”

“Let’s remind them that these people up there in Washington are trying to make you feel powerless,” Harris added. “They’re trying to make you feel alone. They’re trying to make you feel like you don’t have somebody. You have Scott!”

Harris took only 38 percent of the vote in the 2024 presidential election, while President Donald Trump won 60.9 percent.

The former vice president did not flip any counties that Trump carried in 2020, according to an analysis of county-level results from Sabato’s Crystal Ball at the University of Virginia Center for Politics.

She did not stray from taking aim at Trump in her speech, calling him a “tyrant” that Republicans won’t stand up to.

“We are witnessing the most callous, corrupt, and incompetent presidential administration,” Harris said. “We spent the last year and a half looking at TV, saying words we don’t say in church.”

When Colom was on stage, he challenged Trump to debate him when the president visits Corinth, Mississippi, on Oct. 26 because his opponent, whom he nicknamed “Cindy High Prices,” had not debated him.

He quipped that even if people wanted to see Trump speak, they wouldn’t be able to afford the gas to get there.

news.title: US midterms 2026: Why its a do-or-die fight for Trump & the Democracts - explained
news.text: On November 3, Americans will decide whether President Donald Trump gets two more years of a US Congress largely on his side or faces an opposition with the power to challenge his agenda at every turn.All 435 members of the House of Representatives (the lower chamber of Congress) will be elected, while 35 of 100 seats in the Senate (the upper chamber) will also be up for grabs, making the 2026 US midterm elections a critical test of Trump's presidency.Republicans currently control both chambers, giving the White House a clear path to advance its legislative priorities. Democrats are fighting to break that hold, turn Congress into a check on presidential power and reshape the political landscape ahead of the 2028 presidential race.The stakes extend well beyond Capitol Hill as the outcome could determine how far Trump can push his domestic agenda, how aggressively his administration is scrutinised and who sets the terms of America's political debate for the next two years.The US midterm electionsAmericans vote for president and vice president every four years. The four‑year period during which US presidents hold office is called a 'term'.A 'midterm' election is an election that takes place halfway through the presidential term, that is, two years after the presidential elections. They happen across all states, and they are for offices other than that of the president or vice president.Unlike a presidential election, in which voters choose the president through the Electoral College system, the midterms determine the composition of Congress and several important state-level offices.Historically, the president’s party often loses congressional seats in these elections, as voters use the ballot to express satisfaction or frustration with the administration.That pattern is not a guarantee of defeat. But it makes the midterms an important political test for every president, particularly one whose party controls both chambers.The new Congress, known as the 120th Congress, will convene in January 2027. Its composition will determine how much room Trump has to pursue his priorities during the remaining two years of his presidency.The House of RepresentativesThe House is where the battle for congressional control is expected to be particularly intense.Republicans entered the election cycle with a narrow majority. A September 2026 analysis by the European Parliament’s research service put the House balance at 219 Republicans to 214 Democrats, with two vacancies. Reuters reported on October 12 that Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take control.That is a relatively small number in a chamber of 435 members. But winning those seats requires Democrats to prevail in individual districts with distinct political identities, local concerns and candidates.The party seeking to take control must also contend with congressional district boundaries. Mid-decade redistricting, in which states redraw congressional maps between the usual ten-year census cycles, has changed the competitive landscape. Republican-led redistricting efforts have created additional challenges for Democrats in some states, while other districts remain vulnerable to shifts in voter sentiment.The seats that matterWith control of the chamber at stake, a handful of competitive House races could determine whether Republicans retain the power to advance Trump’s agenda or Democrats win the gavel, opening the door to investigations, subpoenas and a fresh confrontation with the White House.The stakes are especially high in a narrow band of battleground districts, where vulnerable Republican incumbents and open seats could decide the outcome.Other races worth watching include contests in Pennsylvania, Arizona, Michigan, North Carolina, Florida and Washington. These states contain districts where narrow margins, candidate-specific factors and the national political climate could determine the outcome.The broader significance is that Democrats do not need to win every competitive district. They need to assemble a majority by gaining enough seats while defending their own vulnerable incumbents.If Republicans retain the House, Trump would preserve a crucial source of legislative support.If Democrats win it, the president would face a chamber controlled by the opposition, changing the relationship between the White House and Congress.The SenateThe Senate is arguably the more consequential prize in terms of appointments and the long-term balance of power in Washington.Republicans currently hold 53 seats, compared with 47 held by Democrats and independents who caucus with them. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to reach a majority of 51. Because the vice-president can break a 50-50 tie, the precise arithmetic can depend on the composition of the chamber and who holds the vice-presidency.The challenge for Democrats is geographical. Several of the most important Republican-held seats are in states that Trump won comfortably in 2024. Democrats must therefore defend their own vulnerable seats while making gains in places where the president remains politically influential.The seats that matterAccording to Reuters' October 12 assessment, the decisive contests include Georgia, Michigan, New Hampshire, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio, Alaska, Iowa, Texas and Kansas.Two other contests deserve attention.In Alaska, Republican Senator Dan Sullivan faces former Democratic Representative Mary Peltola in a state that Trump won by 13 percentage points in 2024. Alaska's ranked-choice voting system adds another layer of complexity.In Iowa, Republican Ashley Hinson and Democrat Josh Turek are competing for an open seat after Senator Joni Ernst decided not to seek re-election. Economic concerns and the Iran war have become part of the debate there.Kansas has also emerged as a race to watch. Republican Senator Roger Marshall faces Democrat Adam Hamilton, with immigration enforcement becoming a point of disagreement within the Republican camp. The contest demonstrates how a national issue can complicate a race even in a state Trump won comfortably.The Senate outcome will matter beyond ordinary legislation. The chamber confirms federal judges, Supreme Court nominees and senior executive appointments.A Republican majority would preserve Trump's ability to seek confirmation of his nominees with support from his own party, subject to Senate rules and individual senators' votes. A Democratic majority would give the opposition much greater leverage over those decisions.It would not automatically allow Democrats to reverse every Trump policy. But it could fundamentally change which appointments proceed, which bills receive consideration and how the administration negotiates with Congress.The governors' racesThe congressional contests will dominate headlines, but voters will also choose governors in 36 states.Going into the election, there are 26 Republican governors and 24 Democratic governors in the United States. This class of governors is made up of 18 Republicans and 18 Democrats. Republicans are defending two governorships in states that Kamala Harris won in 2024 (New Hampshire and Vermont). Democrats are defending five governorships in states that Donald Trump won in 2024 (Arizona, Kansas, Michigan, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin).These elections determine who leads state governments, sets budget priorities and signs or vetoes legislation on issues that directly affect people's lives.Governors can influence healthcare, education, public safety, energy development and the implementation of federal policies. Their administrations also play important roles in emergency management and the conduct of elections under state law.Several contests carry particular national significance.Georgia: The race between Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms and Republican Rick Jackson has implications for policy in a major swing state, including healthcare and the regulation of data centres. Georgia also remains politically significant because of the disputes over the 2020 election.Ohio: Democrat Amy Acton and Republican Vivek Ramaswamy are competing in a state where the governor can influence state policy and election administration.Wisconsin: Democrat David Crowley faces Republican Tom Tiffany. The contest is important in a state that has repeatedly been closely divided in presidential elections.Nevada: The governor's contest is among the races attracting national attention in a state where economic pressures and the cost of living are important political issues.These races are not simply referendums on Trump. State candidates have their own records, constituencies and policy priorities. Nevertheless, their outcomes can shape how national political disputes play out locally and how the parties prepare for 2028.The state legislative contests are equally important.Control of a state legislature can determine whether a governor's proposals become law, whether abortion restrictions are tightened or relaxed, and how election rules are administered. State governments may also have opportunities to redraw congressional maps, depending on their laws and the timing of redistricting.What issues will decide the election?The contests may be local, but the arguments being made in campaign advertisements and at rallies increasingly revolve around the national political climate.A Pew Research Center survey of registered voters conducted between September 28 and October 4 offers a useful snapshot of the issues shaping the election.The economy was rated very important by 84% of registered voters, followed by the future of democracy, healthcare and education. Immigration and foreign policy were also significant concerns.The economy and cost of livingThe economy is the common ground between otherwise sharply divided electorates. Inflation, housing costs, energy prices and the cost of everyday necessities can influence how voters assess the party in power.For Republicans, the election provides an opportunity to argue that the administration's policies are delivering results and that continued congressional control is needed to sustain them. Democrats, by contrast, can use economic dissatisfaction to question whether the administration has adequately addressed household pressures.The Iran conflict adds another dimension. Rising fuel costs and concerns about the economic consequences of the war have become part of the political debate, including in traditionally Republican states. The extent to which voters connect these pressures to the president's policies could influence competitive congressional races.Immigration and border enforcementImmigration remains a central part of Trump's political programme, particularly his efforts to expand deportations and intensify enforcement.Republicans can argue that stronger enforcement is necessary to control illegal immigration and protect national security. Democrats have challenged aspects of the administration's approach, including enforcement practices and their effects on communities, workers and families.The issue is not necessarily a simple Republican advantage. Pew found that 72% of voters supporting Republican congressional candidates considered immigration very important to their vote, compared with 53% of Democratic-candidate supporters. But immigration enforcement has also generated disagreements among Republicans about how far the administration should go.Healthcare, education and abortionHealthcare is another major dividing line, with 82% of Democratic-candidate supporters in the Pew survey describing it as very important to their vote, compared with 53% of Republican-candidate supporters.The election could affect debates over healthcare funding, insurance coverage and the implementation of federal policy. Education, meanwhile, remains important to both parties, although their priorities differ over school governance, curriculum and the role of government.Abortion continues to be politically relevant after the Supreme Court's 2022 decision overturning the constitutional protection previously recognised under Roe v. Wade. State governments have gained greater power to determine abortion policy, making gubernatorial and state legislative contests consequential even where congressional races receive more attention.Democracy, investigations and foreign policyThe future of democracy was rated very important by 73% of registered voters in Pew's survey. The issue encompasses election administration, political accountability and confidence in democratic institutions.For Democratic voters, investigations into the Trump administration are also a significant concern: 63% of Democratic-candidate supporters rated that issue very important, compared with 7% of Republican-candidate supporters.Foreign policy presents another test. The Iran war, tariffs and America's role abroad can influence views about presidential leadership, national security and economic priorities. The election will not itself determine the outcome of any conflict, but it could change the political constraints under which the administration conducts foreign policy.Why the results will matter for 2028Although the next presidential election is still two years away, the midterms will influence how both parties prepare for it.For Republicans, retaining Congress would provide evidence that the party has maintained support during Trump's second term. Losing either chamber would raise questions about the administration's political strategy, its economic record and its ability to mobilise voters beyond its core supporters.For Democrats, winning the House or Senate would provide a platform from which to challenge Trump while helping the party's emerging leaders build national profiles. The results could also intensify internal debates over the party's direction, including the balance between progressive candidates and more centrist figures.The results may therefore shape the environment in which the next presidential contest takes place.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
news.summary: Scheduled for November 3, the US midterm elections are poised to significantly influence the current Trump administration. All 435 House seats and 35 Senate positions are up for grabs, making Congressional control pivotal for advancing Trump's policy goals. Voter priorities like the economy, immigration, healthcare, and democracy are expected to heavily sway electoral outcomes, shaping both immediate governance and the political landscape ahead of the 2028 presidential election.

news.title: Vivek Ramaswamy Is Set for a Historic Flameout in Ohio. I Went to See How It All Went Wrong.
news.text:
The mood at the Vivek Ramaswamy rally was upbeat—confident, even—but the cracks started to show before it began.

The town hall in the small Cleveland suburb of Parma was entitled “Pierogis, Pabst, and Patriots,” and there were plenty of all three on hand at the Union House Bar and Restaurant. But we weren’t really supposed to be here. We were supposed to have convened at the Cleveland Harley-Davidson outpost for a “Christians, Bikers & Patriots” campaign event, before a sudden cancellation necessitated a shift to this woodsy sports joint. There was no word on what had gone wrong with the bikers.

Still, the energy was real in this crimson-tinged bar, bustling with elderly Ohioans in OSU jerseys and MAGA merch alongside watery tubs of PBR. (Among the T-shirts: a red-ink outline of Charlie Kirk raising his fist, and a Trump-Vance shirt where the year was crossed out and replaced, in Sharpie, with 2028.) Alfred, a 60-year-old Filipino immigrant who was raised in Shaker Heights and works in the Parma public school system, told me he didn’t think, whatever the national narrative, that too many of his fellow conservatives were disaffected with Donald Trump or the current Republican Party. He loved the way Immigration and Customs Enforcement was operating, and anyway, as devout Catholics, he and his wife would never vote for a pro-choice Democrat like Amy Acton—Ramaswamy’s opponent in the bitter race for the Ohio governor’s mansion. Others I spoke to were similarly unbothered. Mark, a retired Air Force technician sitting at the bar, was planning on attending church that very evening and claimed to be far more concerned about property taxes than Ramaswamy’s Hinduism, one of the many issues that may work against the candidate in this very Christian state. To him, Ramaswamy’s religious objectors were just “morons who say stupid shit.”

Once the actual event kicked off, however, even the speakers couldn’t help but strike notes of concern. “If you choose not to decide in this election, you are supporting a cast of characters that wants to take our state in a fundamentally dangerous direction,” said Secretary of State Frank LaRosa, invoking Rush’s “Freewill” as he opened for the guest of honor and promoted his own campaign for state auditor. “The Democrats are feelin’ chippy,” he warned. “But there will be no blue wave. There will be a bright-red Ramaswamy tsunami!”

Ramaswamy finally took the stump to raucous applause and harped on his finely honed campaign planks—improving public schools, reducing property taxes and everyday costs, welcoming legal immigrants—while firing some culture-war drive-bys at the evils of “wokeism” and “transgenderism.” Former Ohio Treasurer Josh Mandel subsequently took the mic and felt the need to emphasize Ramaswamy’s devotion to God. “I’ve been with Vivek at churches all over the state. There’s this band of Christian warriors who are following and supporting Vivek because he supports them,” Mandel stressed.

The sentiment proved to be a bellwether for the audience Q&A. An answer Ramaswamy gave condemning sanctuary cities wasn’t enough for a hoarse-voiced attendee who repeatedly interrupted: “Damned immigrants are hurtin’ everybody! We gotta get all of ’em out of here!”

Ramaswamy stumbled for a moment, responding that legal immigrants were still cool, which failed to satisfy the heckler. “All of ’em!” the attendee yelled. “Send in the military!”

Not long after, a separate dissident followed up, skipping over the queue to ask, twice, “Do you believe Jesus is God?”

“Sir, we’re going to ask you to be respectful,” Ramaswamy replied.

“It’s a simple question!” the old man yelled back.

“We don’t reward those who are just screaming for attention,” Ramaswamy replied, turning away from the troublemaker. The supportive crowd handed another microphone to a Republican-voting teacher who’d earlier objected to one of Ramaswamy’s screeds about the current state of education in the state, and asked a question about his commitment to ensuring that all Ohio kids, including those with disabilities, learn to read. Here, despite the criticism, the candidate sounded a warmer note.

“We’ll be respectful to anyone who has a tough question,” Ramaswamy declared. “If I can’t stand up here and answer a tough question, then I have no business running the state.”

The problem for him is that there are nothing but tough questions, and he may not have good answers for many of them. If you believe the polls, it seems clear that Ramaswamy—a Cincinnati-born disciple of the MAGA political school, biotech entrepreneur, and one-time Republican presidential candidate—could be the first Ohio Republican to lose a gubernatorial bid in 20 years. The once swingy Buckeye State has only reddened further since Donald Trump flipped it in his first presidential bid, and the MAGA movement’s heir apparent, Vice President J.D. Vance, famously hails from here. Yet this could be the state where Ramaswamy, who once pitched himself as a younger and more capable Trump, ends up buckling to Acton, a doctor and first-time candidate who led Ohio’s Department of Health in the early days of its COVID response. There are a lot of reasons for this: He’s a pro–data center billionaire running for office at a moment when even Republican super PAC ads are pillorying billionaires and data centers. His Harvard-and-Yale pedigree and debate-me-bro verbosity make him come off more like a snob than a man of the people. He gets heckled a lot, even amid ostensibly friendly crowds. The social media posts where he does try to present himself as down-to-earth are frequently subjected to viral mockery. He doesn’t seem to be able to activate Republicans in a year when Buckeye Dems are actually motivated to hit the polls. The messages from his campaign, and from his well-funded supporters, have taken some incredibly vicious tacks—including, most recently and notoriously, an ad featuring the support of Acton’s estranged mother, who stayed married to a man whom the Democrat accused of sexually abusing her as a child.

And then, most obviously of all: Ramaswamy is a dark-skinned Hindu with a lengthy (and self-admittedly “funny-sounding”) last name who’s vying to be the standard-bearer of a party whose members increasingly present themselves as anti-Indian, anti-Hindu warriors for the Christian white identity project.

In Ohio, I was trying to surmise just how much Ramaswamy’s ethnicity and religion were helping usher in his political demise in this GOP. What I saw surprised me. There were scenes like the one at the rally, where some Republicans’ anti-immigrant, pro–Christian America rhetoric played out more familiarly. But among Ramaswamy’s fellow South Asians, a demographic that votes broadly Democratic but has drifted a touch rightward in recent cycles, there is also widespread doubt and suspicion—inconvenient for a campaign that needs every vote it can find. The community ties and social connections that Ramaswamy and his family have established across Cincinnati and Columbus could be helpful, in theory. But for many of his would-be constituents, the question is what those connections mean when the candidate has embraced a movement that sees them as the enemy. If you want to understand why Ramaswamy seems on course for a historic crashout in Ohio, those voters are a good place to start.

In 2024, Amjad Baig, a real estate agent based in the Columbus suburbs, joined an unusual coalition of Americans in making a counterintuitive choice: He voted for Donald Trump.

Baig, who supported Hillary Clinton in 2016 and organized a Pakistanis for Biden group in 2020, considers himself a fervent patriot. After emigrating from Lahore to the United States in the early 2000s and settling in the Ohio town of Dublin, the 54-year-old father of four got involved with its burgeoning South Asian blocs, eventually becoming president of the local Community Association of Pakistani Americans, and partnering frequently with the Ohio branch of the Federation of Indian Associations. I met him in September for dinner at Neehee’s, a regional Indian chain, where he recounted his Trump-era political journey.

“Joe Biden should have resigned earlier. Six months before the election, they decided Kamala Harris would run as a candidate. There was no primary,” he said. “We could have had a better candidate. So I encouraged people in my network to vote against Harris.” They weren’t hard to persuade, Baig added: Many South Asian Ohioans were already angered by the Biden administration’s indifference toward the atrocities in Gaza, and partial to Trump’s publicly professed skepticism of Middle Eastern wars.

That’s not quite how things have turned out two years later. Israel is still bombing Gaza, despite the ostensible ceasefire with Hamas; the war in Iran and its price shocks continue, hitting everything from fuel to food; Trump 2.0 is persecuting immigrants far more thoroughly, and aggressively, than even in his first term. The normally independent-minded South Asians across Ohio’s cities, Baig told me, are so furious that they’re again ready to vote against an Indian American candidate, just to hold Trump to account, even though many of them liked Ramaswamy when he first emerged on the scene.

This western stretch of the Columbus metropolitan area, the fastest-growing and most economically vibrant region in the Buckeye State, is not coincidentally home to its largest South Asian populations. Twenty years ago, as Baig related to me, the Noor Islamic Cultural Center had opened its doors in Dublin, welcoming the burgeoning South Asian American groups who had settled in and around the state’s capital. About a 15-minute drive away stands Ohio’s oldest Hindu temple, founded by white Hare Krishna disciples, now home to hundreds of worshippers of Indian origin. The Noor’s opening similarly attracted an influx of Ohioans with family roots in Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Afghanistan. It’s a collective of freethinking, independent, educated constituents who, across their respective backgrounds and countries of origin, have a lot of thoughts about the fact that one of their own is running to become governor of their state.

As Ohio State University professor Pranav Jani has written, Ramaswamy may be “skinfolk, but so not our kinfolk.” Unfortunately for the campaign, there are many others who feel this way.

“This is a country I need to protect, which is harder to do these days,” Baig told me. He was distressed about quite a few matters: the economic burdens facing Ohio’s small-business owners, national and local restrictions on the voting process, state-level efforts undermining the local hemp industry. Yet one matter was paramount: the attacks on first-generation immigrants like himself.

“We’re scared,” he added. “Just being an immigrant, you’re a target, thanks to ICE and all these bigots who’ve been given permission by Donald Trump. Vivek is going to follow what the Republicans say, and they’re so anti-immigrant now that that’s where he’ll land.”

Shabana Siddiqi, a conservative-leaning but, she said, nonpartisan retired physician who’d appreciated Ramaswamy’s presidential campaign for foregrounding his family background and opposing transgender education in schools, sounded nothing less than contemptuous of him now. “Racism is so common here, especially for Pakistanis and Indians. Vivek is brown, and we are all citizens with the same rights, but he doesn’t care about that,” she said. “I’ve met with Amy. She listens to us. She feels our pain. And I don’t think these Republicans understand, they’re losing a large chunk of votes the way they’re going.”

Aziz Taqdeer, an Afghan immigrant and social worker who’s lived in the United States since 2015, told me he’s hitting the polls for the first time ever because of his concerns around the Trump administration’s immigration crackdowns. “Over the past three years, it’s become impossible to get by. I’ve never been more worried,” Taqdeer said. “I know people who’ve been detained by ICE, and it does something horrible to your mental health, to know these agents can come for you at any time.” Also weighing on Taqdeer’s mind: inflation, his children, the driver who yelled at him the other day to “go back to your country,” and the ongoing betrayal of the many Afghans he knew who assisted U.S. forces against the Taliban.

Across differences in politics and identity, South Asians I spoke with around Columbus also shared the same affordability concerns acutely felt by Americans everywhere. As Baig reminded me, “Many of us are small-business owners, independent workers, homeowners, so we’re even more greatly squeezed by all these rising bills.”

Kashif Mehmood, a fossil-fuel engineer who voted for incumbent Republican Gov. Mike DeWine in 2022, said he will now be voting Democratic across the ballot in large part because of inflation. “I’m right in the center, not on the extreme left or right—I vote for whoever is good for the country,” Mehmood said. “Right now, the war and the economy are in such a horrible place. It’s making things harder for all us.”

Rajnikanth Katte, a Hindu Indian immigrant who serves as chairman of the Federation of Indian Associations in Ohio, agreed with this diagnosis and suspected that Democrats would win, even as he proudly displayed to me a photo of himself standing with LaRose, the secretary of state, at a recent federation event. “So many people are struggling and hurting right now,” Katte said. “I’m always in favor of whoever can help us make incremental improvements—whoever it is, whether that’s a Democrat or a Republican, I’ll support them.”

This will be the first election in Ohio’s history in which neither of the major-party gubernatorial candidates is Christian. (If she wins, Acton will be the first Jewish governor.) The large majority of Ohioans are Christian, and a quarter of them identify squarely as evangelical. Hindu, Jewish, and Muslim Buckeyes each make up 1 percent of the population, while nearly 30 percent of the state professes no religious affiliation, according to the Pew Research Center. White evangelicals still retain influence in Ohio, and they’ve made clear they do not love either of the choices they have in this race.

Throughout the year, Ramaswamy has been dogged by a resurfaced clip from his presidential run in which he tells an Iowa voter that Jesus is a son of God, not the son. That comment earned an early-year denunciation from Cincinnati pastor Michael Clary, who scoffed at the idea that “Vishnu worshipers could hold public office” and tweeted that he’d vote for Ramaswamy’s main opponent in the Republican gubernatorial primary: Casey Putsch, a car mechanic who also attacked Ramaswamy over his Hindu faith and invited the candidate to play “Cowboys and Indians” in a campaign ad where he fired off his rifle. After Putsch lost, Christian nationalist preacher Joel Webbon begged on his podcast for Republicans to stay home and send a message to the GOP that its base doesn’t want “polytheistic, demon-worshiping, cow-worshiping, bare-feet, scamming anchor baby Indians” in office.

Many Christian Ohioans don’t believe that Ramaswamy’s Hinduism is disqualifying—though that’s not to say they think anyone of any other faith should hold office, whatever the Constitution may say about religious freedom. Philip Coon, a retired industrial salesman who lives west of Dayton, is a MAGA Christian who thinks “Trump’s going to hell” and needs to “shut his mouth,” though that doesn’t depress his political support. “I’m hiring Trump to run the country, not to be my pastor,” Coon told me. “It’s the same thing with Vivek: I’m hiring him to run the state. I wish he was Christian, but he’s not.” Still, that openness does have a limit. “At my steel company, I dealt with Muslims, I dealt with Indians, and I got along with all of them. I hope they were legal, because I loved them,” he told me. “But I’m anti-Islam as far as this: I don’t think Muslims should get in our government because that’s bad news. I do believe the Antichrist is going to be Muslim.”

Others have been even more direct. A Chester-based preacher named John Young has repeatedly posted his “Ohio Must Stand on Godly Principles” essay below multiple Ramaswamy campaign Facebook posts, writing that he cannot support either contender because “our allegiance belongs first to Jesus Christ, not to a political party.” (Others tend to parrot that sentiment on Instagram whenever Ramaswamy shares a photo from a religious function.) When Baptist preacher and state Rep. Gary Click invited Ramaswamy to his church for a town hall, he ended up engaging in petty social media battles with followers who claimed they “never thought I would ever see a Baptist minister support a Hindu for Governor.” Younger Republicans deeply attached to the idea of America as a Christian nation appear little interested in seeking kinship with a millennial who doesn’t share their particular bent, no matter how MAGA he may otherwise be.

“I had students who went to a Turning Point rally in April, out of interest, and the report I heard was that there were very few other young folks at the event,” Benjamin McKean, an associate professor of political theory at Ohio State University, told me. “I have students who are excited about Vivek and Trump. But they’re cognizant of the fact that most students do not share their enthusiasm. It’s hard to compete with a frat party or whatever if the alternative is to go hear Vivek talk about why he still supports Israel.”

The one promising sign for Ramaswamy this election is that the older, whiter retirees of faith who showed up with such enthusiasm in Parma tend to be the most reliable voters around. And there are religious leaders loudly making it known they’ll vote for him, if reluctantly. “I would prefer to have a Christian on the ballot for governor in Ohio this year,” wrote Crossroads Baptist Church pastor Neal Daryan in a letter to the Columbus Dispatch. “Vivek Ramaswamy holds my Christian values, and I’m voting for him.”

Still, for anyone remaining on the fence, it might not help that some of the pastors who’ve put their support behind Ramaswamy are steeped in controversy. Jeff Tauring, a preacher who helped host the Parma event I attended, is notorious for leading a congregation that once protested outside a Jewish Democratic lawmaker’s house in 2022 with a banner commanding the legislator to “kneel before the cross.” In August, just before Ramaswamy spoke at a Middletown church, its pastor dismissed the possibility of hosting a similar event with Amy Acton, because “you wouldn’t ask a Muslim church to host a pork festival, would you?”

Acton is most likely to gain the support of religious minorities, along with more-liberal Christians and unaffiliated voters, if they’re fired up to vote against Ramaswamy. (So far, early voting numbers suggest they are.) That, of course, includes the very Hindus whose beliefs Ramaswamy so frequently invokes. Meanwhile, the Republicans of faith who voted for Putsch’s bigoted campaign could follow his lead in refusing to endorse the man who beat him. The depressed MAGA turnout is what’s most worrying Ramaswamy’s running mate, state Senate President Rob McColley. “We have three opponents right now in this race: We have Amy Acton, we have the national political environment, and then we have complacency,” McColley told a group of Republicans in the spring. “I would argue the third opponent is the most dangerous opponent we possibly have.”

One thing that Amjad Baig, the 2024 Trump voter and community organizer, kept making clear to me is that in everyday life, he’s not a partisan, and he prefers it that way. He owns multiple Teslas, and neither Elon Musk’s white supremacist turn nor his massive donations on behalf of Ramaswamy’s campaign will get Baig to join liberals’ Tesla boycotts. (His Dublin neighborhood is, incidentally, located next to a Tesla collision center.) He counts a few local GOP operatives, including volunteers for the Ramaswamy campaign, among his personal friends. He even found Ramaswamy to be an interesting guy, back when he was making waves in the 2023 GOP field.

But Baig also does like Amy Acton, whom he’s met multiple times. He’s likewise realistic about what he’ll be voting for when he votes for her. “Acton is very genuine and very liberal,” he said. “But the only reason she will win is because people don’t want Vivek.”

That can go multiple ways. People don’t want Vivek, meaning onetime GOP voters are fed up and sticking it to the party. People don’t want Vivek, meaning strict Christians don’t want a Hindu in office. People don’t want Vivek, meaning they think immigrants and their citizen-by-birth children are ruining America. In Ohio, I saw all versions in action. (His campaign did not respond to my requests for comment for this piece, and members of the press were not allowed to ask any questions of the candidate at the Parma town hall.)

This week, the outcry over the campaign ad with Acton’s mother has especially intensified, reminding the wider country of its aversion to Ramaswamy. (The already-unpopular president, who has defended the ad and reportedly told the candidate to “say thank you, God” for the get, might not be helping.) I’ve been thinking about what Shabana Siddiqi, the retired physician, told me in Dublin: that Acton “listens” and “feels our pain” when it comes to the horrors that immigrants and South Asians have faced during Trump’s second term. There was nothing like that forward-facing sense of understanding or empathy when she first encountered Ramaswamy during his presidential run. And from the viewpoint of her community, Acton was hardly the person all those Ramaswamy campaign ads alleged her to be: a drug and alcohol addict who championed such far-reaching stay-at-home pandemic orders during her Health Department tenure that she left countless Ohioans scarred.

“This negative campaigning is so ugly,” Siddiqi said. “All these ads are just against the other person. You don’t know who they are, or what they believe.” At least, until she met Acton for herself and made her own judgment.

So, yes, Ramaswamy’s Hindu faith may not be welcomed by many of Ohio’s Christians. But even among Ohio’s South Asians, of all beliefs, Ramaswamy’s entreaties to that dogma simply do not jibe with his actual conduct as a candidate, from his alignment with an intolerant political movement to his willingness to indulge in constant, personal attacks on his opponent.

Sudarshan Pyakurel, a Columbus resident and Hindu Bhutanese refugee, wrote a column for the Columbus Dispatch back in January where he called out Ramaswamy over that. “Many Hindu families in Ohio live with fear—fear of ICE raids, profiling based on accent or appearance and the constant anxiety of family separation,” Pyakurel wrote. “In such a moment, a public figure who claims Hindu values but offers only rhetoric and silence does not represent us.”

A lot of people don’t want Vivek. That may include a lot of intolerant Ohioans—but it will also, pointedly, include his own skinfolk.
news.summary: The voters who are against him tell the story.

news.title: Arizona man sentenced for threatening to 'execute' Trump — and Kamala Harris
news.text:
An Arizona man was sentenced to a little more than three years in prison for threatening to "execute" President Donald Trump and Kamala Harris.

Rene Ortiz of Casa Grande issued the written threats on Election Day in 2024, according to a press release from the U.S. Attorney's Office in Arizona.

He wrote that he would shoot 'the incoming fraudulent elected [President of the United States] … at the inauguration on January 20th, 2025.'

The 56-year-old wrote a note asserting that he would "execute the newly elected [President of the United States] by firing an M-16A2 service rifle with a magazine of 6 rounds" and delivered it to the federal courthouse in Phoenix.

That threat was directed at both candidates, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office.

After Trump won, Ortiz issued another written threat that was delivered to the federal courthouse in Tucson.

In that threat, he wrote that he would shoot "the incoming fraudulent elected [President of the United States] ... at the inauguration on January 20th, 2025."

Ortiz was interviewed by U.S. Secret Service, and he reiterated his intent to attack the president.

He was arrested on Jan. 17, 2025, before the presidential inauguration.

Ortiz was convicted by a federal jury on June 8 and was sentenced by Senior U.S. District Judge Stephen M. McNamee on Tuesday.

More recently, a 24-year-old man named Jaden Read was arrested after posting on social media that he would kill the president when he visited Kansas.

news.title: ‘26 Must Add to ‘32  | Opinion
news.text: With the midterms only about two weeks away, all focus is on the Election Day 2026 races. The Democrats appear as if they will flip the House of Representatives and are increasingly looking as if they are poised to flip the Senate as well. The Senate races in particular are getting an enormous amount of attention. However, the gubernatorial races in key states are getting much less focus, and in these last two weeks there needs to be an extra push in those races to help prepare for 2032. What do the current elections for governor have to do with presidential politics in 2032? Potentially a lot, and here is why. There will be a new United States population census in 2030. This obviously will not affect the next presidential cycle two years from now, but it will very much affect the makeup of the Electoral College vote six years from now. That is because current red states are expected to pick up several House seats and current blue states are projected to lose seats in the 2030 population count. That will correspond directly to a gain and loss in Electoral College votes among the states. To put that in total perspective, the South is expected to have double the number of House seats as the Northeast with 164 versus 81. Texas is projected to gain as many as four Electoral College votes, and Florida two or three, while California is expected to lose four such votes. In addition, solid red states Utah and Idaho would pick up one more vote, while solid blue states New York, Illinois, Oregon, and Rhode Island would each lose one. Moreover, northern swing states Minnesota, Wisconsin, and Pennsylvania would lose one vote and southern swing states Georgia, North Carolina, and Arizona would each gain one. This is not a simple story of red states gaining and blue states losing population, because one needs to look at the underlying reasons for those gains and losses to really assess what kind of electoral headwinds the Democrats are facing. And there are some reasons for Democrats to be more positive than the headline numbers on population shifts alone might suggest. There are four key reasons populations shift among the states: birth and death rates, migration between states, immigration from abroad and census counting efforts. Examining each provides meaningful insight into whether gains for traditionally red states will necessarily translate into a political advantage for Republicans. According to The Economist, birth rates are higher in counties that typically vote Republican than in those that typically vote Democratic. However, Republican-leaning counties skew older and have significantly higher death rates. As a result, life expectancy in Democratic counties is over three years longer than in Republican counties. Deaths now actually outnumber births in Republican-leaning counties, resulting in negative natural population growth, while natural growth remains positive in Democratic counties. Looking at migration between the states, The Economist also reports that migration from other states has increased the population in Republican counties by an average of 0.5 percent a year, while Democratic counties have tended to lose population as residents move elsewhere by about 0.6 percent per year. What somewhat mitigates this for Democrats is that about 20 percent of the new arrivals in red states come from blue states and around 40 percent come from swing states, which has weakened the amount of Republican support in the fastest-growing red counties. This suggests that many of those moving from blue states are bringing their politics with them. When it comes to immigration from abroad, the trend adds to population growth about five times more in blue counties than red ones. But immigration contributes heavily to population growth in red states. Immigration has accounted for 44 percent of Texas’ population growth over the last two years, more than came from domestic migration or natural population increases. That is even more true when it comes to Florida. Of course, immigrants cannot vote, but they are counted for census purposes, although the Trump administration would like to change that. In doing so, however, it may actually reduce the Electoral College advantage that would otherwise flow to certain Republican states. In fact, if immigration remains at zero or turns negative for the rest of the decade, Florida's Electoral College gain could be limited to two additional votes rather than three. Florida may also see a sharp decline in migration from other states as rising housing costs make it increasingly unaffordable for retirees. It is not only population growth but the ethnic and racial composition of that growth that matters for electoral purposes. For example, in Texas, population growth in the Houston and Dallas areas has been driven almost entirely by the growth of communities of color, a trend expected to continue in the coming years. Similarly, in Georgia, communities of color are the only groups experiencing population growth, according to The New York Times. Lastly, population counts may be further affected by what actions states take in trying to promote the importance of filling out census forms, particularly in immigrant communities. New York and California spent significant sums encouraging residents to do so, while Texas spent no state funds on such outreach. It has been estimated as a result that Texas actually received fewer House seats, and therefore fewer Electoral College votes to cast, based on the 2020 census. Adding a citizenship question to the census forms, as the Trump administration looks like it will attempt to do again in preparation for the 2030 census, might further depress the immigration population growth in red and blue states alike as immigrants become fearful of the use of that information. With all these puts and takes, even if the Democrats were to lose blue state voting power in the Electoral College, there are some underlying population trends working to their advantage in red state America. However, the bottom line is that even if the Dems win the Rust Belt swing states of Michigan, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin in 2032—which they narrowly lost to Trump in 2024—while holding all the other states that Kamala Harris carried, based on the expected population shifts they would still lose the Electoral College by 20 votes. That means they would have to win either North Carolina, Georgia, or Arizona to get to the clinching number of 270 votes. To the extent they lost any of the Rust Belt states, they will need two or more southern states to prevail. What is the import of this for the 2026 races? It means Democrats must win governorships that are up for grabs in states like Georgia, Florida, and Texas to begin rebuilding the on-the-ground party infrastructure needed to make these increasingly important Electoral College states competitive. With underlying population trends—on natural population growth, the political leanings of migrating populations from other states, and racial composition of growing populations—helping to potentially shift southern states closer to Democratic voting majorities, Democrats need to build back their party infrastructure in these states. They have in many cases left their state party apparatus to atrophy, particularly when it comes to fundraising and getting out the vote. Winning state governorships has an awful lot to do with making the necessary repairs. Those governor races in Georgia, Florida, and Texas where Democrats have a real chance of flipping those offices this year need money badly right now. In this way, ‘26 can really add to ‘32. Tom Rogers is executive chairman of the AI film studio Fountain 0, executive chairman of agentic AI company Claigrid, Inc., the founder of CNBC, an on-air CNBC contributor, a member of the Task Force for American Democracy. The views expressed in this article are the writer's own.

news.title: Elon Musk Blows Fuse Over Calls For Potential Investigations Into Him: 'I Will Find Out'
news.text:
Tech trillionaire Elon Musk appeared concerned on Wednesday about burgeoning calls for lawmakers to investigate him should Democrats flip the House or Senate in the upcoming midterms, reacting on social media to reports and critics with varying levels of ire.

He seemed particularly troubled by a new Politico report titled “Capitol Agenda: Dem Gavels Are Coming for Elon Musk,” on House Democrats in their purported quest to investigate Musk over his time as head of the so-called Department of Government Efficiency or DOGE.

“Live by the sword, die by the sword,” Musk wrote on Wednesday on X while resharing the article. “Those who pick fights with me should understand that I will find out who is really pulling the strings and come for them, not just their puppets …”

The Tesla and SpaceX CEO spearheaded DOGE under US President Donald Trump in a stated effort to slash wasteful public spending, only to dismantle numerous key agencies, including the Department of Education and USAID, which administered civilian foreign aid.

Musk, whose companies receive billions in federal contracts, has also been accused of using DOGE to gut regulatory agencies that were investigating his businesses. The X owner seemed irate on Wednesday at the notion, according to tech journalist Kara Swisher.

He commented on a clip of her remarks, “Sounds like Swisher really wants to go to prison.”

Swisher argued during an appearance on The Bulwark podcast “Receipts” that Musk would already be in jail if former Vice President Kamala Harris won the 2024 election, warning “if Donald Trump loses the House and the Senate, I would worry … no matter how rich he is.”

She added, “There were all these agencies, some of which he put a knife in and killed in the DOGE, many of whom were investigating him. He stopped like half a dozen investigations of his various companies. So they’re gonna start investigating again. You think he’s not on the list?”

Swisher continued, “He’s at the top of that list. Donald Trump obviously is at the top, and his family ... but Elon Musk is right up there for that ... He knows what’s coming. Like, he’s not stupid. Of all the many things you can say about him is he has a very big sense of fate.”

She concluded, “And I think it’s coming for him. And real hard.”

The Wall Street Journal on Wednesday reported that Musk last week personally ordered his network of Starlink satellites slowed in Ukraine amid Russia’s ongoing invasion there, and Democrats have kept an eye on his potentially unconstitutional actions at DOGE.

Musk has claimed that the military version of Starlink being used in the region is solely owned and operated by the US government, and that any “limits on speed or usage” are decided by the military “and ultimately POTUS,” meaning Trump.

While it remains to be seen if the world’s richest man will face actual investigations following the midterms, Musk seemingly reacted to the Journal story Wednesday by writing on X, “Some fools still think the legacy news is real. Amazing.”

The article’s co-author, Alex Ward, responded on X, writing, “Sir, is this your comment to our story?”

news.title: Veterans Facing the Battle of the Ballot Box
news.text:
Veterans Day isn’t for another few weeks, but it’s worth taking a closer look at veterans in the run-up to the November 3 elections. There are just under 17 million living veterans in America, according to the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, comprising about six percent of the electorate. In a close election, they can determine the outcome of any given contest.

Veterans overwhelmingly favored Donald Trump in the last presidential election. A September 30, 2024, survey by Pew Research showed a +24 advantage for Trump over Kamala Harris two years ago. But these midterm elections are very different, given the number of candidates up and down the ballot who openly campaign on socialist issues and who are adjacent to extremist Islamist organizations. Why does this matter?

Of those 17 million veterans, about 30,000 served during World War II. Most of the remainder fought in Korea, Vietnam, the Cold War, and various Middle East conflicts including the Gulf War era, and post-9/11 conflicts in Iraq, Afghanistan, and elsewhere. In every war since 1950, Americans fought against socialism, communism, and an Islamist ideology that promoted global terrorism. The men and women taking up arms against these schools of thought over the past half-century watched their buddies die in combat, suffered the privations of armed conflict, and stood against the enemy with resolve.

Veterans don’t forget their enemies. As a Cold War veteran from the 1970s and ‘80s, I vividly recall hunting Soviet nuclear-armed submarines in the North Atlantic, watching Soviet-made Libyan fighter jets fire on warships in the Gulf of Sidra, and spending more than two months on-station off the coast of Iran in the Arabian Sea. They were prepared to kill us, and we were prepared to kill them. That’s how war works. 

Today, ideologies that animated our enemies over the past 75 years are on the ballot, a fact not likely lost on veterans. The Democratic Socialists of America website lists more than 150 candidates and ballot initiatives they’re supporting this year. The political arm of the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR) website lets people search for its endorsements and preferences state-by-state. Where I live in Texas, CAIR is a designated foreign terrorist organization, along with the Muslim Brotherhood. These people are telling us how to vote. 

For its part, the Muslim Brotherhood is smart enough not to endorse American politicians, but the group has placed Michigan Senate nominee Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed in an uncomfortable position. Between his own public expressions of sympathy for the organization and more direct connections among some of his extended family, it raises legitimate questions. 

This has absolutely nothing to do with what El-Sayed looks like, how he prays, or how his name is spelled. It has everything to do with his pursuit of power over foreign relations should he win his election. He’s already explicitly said Israel is neither an ally nor friend, a highly provocative statement given that the United States was the first government on earth to recognize the nation of Israel in 1948. We’ve been allies ever since. 

How veterans will respond to these midterm election dynamics is unclear. Some will undoubtedly pull the lever for some of these candidates, but a lot of them, probably many more of them, will think to themselves, ‘Wait, didn’t we go to war with these ideas?’ People who believed many of the same things embraced by American politicians today wanted to kill them when they were in uniform. American veterans can be among the most forgiving people among us, including forgiving their past enemies. news.title: Ketanji Brown Jackson Breaks With SCOTUS Voting Order as Election Looms
news.text: Supreme Court Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the sole dissenter in a new Supreme Court order that green-lit New Hampshire to fully ban student IDs for voting during November's midterm elections. In the order, Brown concluded, "I respectfully dissent because—even, and perhaps especially, when an election is looming—I would not disturb a clearly justifiable federal-court order issued to ensure that the public receives accurate information about a State’s electoral processes." New Hampshire passed a law earlier this year that said student IDs were not an acceptable form of identification to get a ballot, the Associated Press (AP) reports. What We Know The High Court's order ultimately blocks students from using their school IDs as a backup, the AP says. New Hampshire's Republican Secretary of State David Scanlan barred the IDs from being an acceptable backup after the state passed the law, the AP reports. A judge first left the law to stand as is but reversed course earlier this month, prompting the emergency appeal. The emergency appeal in Scanlan's case was ultimately granted by the High Court on Thursday. Legal Counsel for The Coalition For Open Democracy, the plaintiff in the case, called the court's order "wrong." "The Court’s decision grants a stay which both the federal district court and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit denied, blocking an injunction that has now been in place for almost three weeks, injecting confusion into the election—precisely what the Purcell principle is supposed to prevent—and authorizing an unconstitutional policy that will deprive young voters of their right to vote. "We applaud Justice Jackson for her dissent, in which she stands for the Constitution, the right to vote, and a rational application of Purcell. We will continue to vigorously litigate this case in the defense of the fundamental right to vote of young voters across New Hampshire," the statement read. The order mentions the Purcell principle, which is a legal concept in election law in the United States that advises courts against altering voting rules too close to an election. The election related ruling comes just 12 days before the midterms. Midterm elections are commonly viewed as a test of the political environment facing the party in power, and the president's party has historically lost seats during them. President Donald Trump lost New Hampshire during the 2024 presidential election to then-Vice President Kamala Harris. news.title: Trump Aides LaCivita, Blair Donate Bosnian Fee to Library
news.text:
WASHINGTON — Chris LaCivita and James Blair, two of President Trump’s election advisers, have donated their six-figure consulting fees from a controversial political assignment in Bosnia and Herzegovina to Trump’s presidential library, The Post has learned.

Trump was “gloating” and “very braggadocious” in private conversations this week after learning about the donation, according to a source. The reaction suggests that his initial anger toward LaCivita and Blair over their work in Eastern Europe has subsided.

A second source also confirmed that Trump was pleased by the donation.

Four sources confirmed the transfer. Two of them said Trump learned of the decision indirectly rather than from LaCivita or Blair themselves.

LaCivita, who co-led Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, and Blair, who served as a White House deputy chief of staff until May, are still likely to owe income taxes on the earnings. Sources said each man received more than $100,000 from the consulting work.

Trump had lashed out earlier this month after The New York Times reported that the pair, who hold senior positions at the MAGA Inc. super PAC, had traveled to support a political party in the ethnically Serbian Republika Srpska. They advised the ruling party, led by Milorad Dodik, during the region’s election, which the party won.

SEE ALSO: Kamala Harris Met With Silence at Mississippi Rally After Quote Flub

Dodik has friendly relationships with both Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The outside assignment created the impression that LaCivita and Blair were using their ties to Trump for personal financial gain while diverting attention from struggling Republican congressional campaigns. Some colleagues, however, said the two men remained involved in the US election effort remotely.

“Chris LaCivita and James Blair are outside consultants. They do not work for me, other than as outside consultants. They most likely have numerous clients, but for that, you would have to ask them,” Trump wrote on Truth Social in his initial response on Oct. 7.

“They are allowed to do work for others, just like all consultants in Washington, D.C. I do not have any idea who else they work for but will, on reflection, ask them and, if there’s a conflict, I will terminate them, immediately!”

Blair, who spearheaded a Republican redistricting effort this year aimed at reshaping House districts to benefit the GOP, joined Trump at a campaign rally in South Carolina on Wednesday. His appearance pointed to a thaw in their relationship.

A White House official told The Post on Thursday that Trump did not appear upset with Blair and was unlikely to hold him responsible if Republicans were wiped out on Nov. 3. The official described the president’s conversations with Blair as businesslike and focused on campaign tactics.

news.title: Hughesy, Karl and co: what happens when celebrities turn political?
news.text:
In recent months, many Australians would have seen or heard celebrities such as Dave Hughes, Karl Stefanovic and Kyle Sandilands becoming more involved in Australia’s political debate.

While it is not new for celebrities to express political opinions, social media has changed how they engage in public debate. 

They can influence people even if they don’t officially endorse a political party or appear at a campaign rally. 

But what is particularly interesting is these personalities are engaging with politics in different ways. 

Capitalising on social grievance

Many Australians are frustrated by cost-of-living pressures, housing affordability and declining trust in political institutions. 

Celebrities often use humour, criticism and relatable commentary to channel those frustrations. 

They position themselves as speaking for ordinary Australians, rather than political elites. Genuine public concerns can be expressed through outrage-driven narratives. 

But this approach can reinforce dissatisfaction rather than encourage informed political debate. For those on the conservative side of the political spectrum who benefit from these engagements, it has been described as “right-wing grifting”.

What are Hughes, Stefanovic and co doing?

Hughes has become increasingly outspoken in his criticism of Labor, focusing on policy and economics. He maintains his political stance is driven by opposition to government mismanagement, rather than opposition to the political left.

He recently attended a Victorian Liberal Party campaign event but stopped his engagement because of concerns it might breach the state’s political donation laws.

Hughes has described himself as a “former lifelong Labor voter”. 

Once one of the highest paid Australian television presenters, Stefanovic has moved further into political commentary through his podcast. 

With guests including political figures and former government officials, he has tackled controversial topics. He recently hosted the conservative CPAC conference in Brisbane. 

Controversial radio host Sandilands is another interesting example, having shifted from his public friendship with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to expressing support for Pauline Hanson and One Nation. 

He claims he even assisted the party with its political messaging, demonstrating how celebrity influence can extend beyond public commentary into political strategy.

More recently, comedian Luke McGregor – who has a degree in economics – has attracted attention for his criticism of the Reserve Bank’s approach to inflation and unemployment. His commentary is more policy-focused than party-politics, demonstrating political influence does not necessarily require an explicit political allegiance.

The changing face of media consumption

These celebrities have all developed relationships with audiences outside politics. Their followers already know their personalities as both celebrities and content creators. 

Audiences understand their humour and may feel a sense of familiarity with them. This creates opportunities to introduce politics into spaces where people might not otherwise actively seek it.

The University of Canberra’s 2026 digital news report highlights how significant the shift towards non-traditional media has become. 

43% of Australian consumers access news from creators and influencers
48% of 18–24 year-olds use TikTok for news
among people consuming influencer-led news, 59% consider it more entertaining, 55% more relatable and 56% easier to understand than traditional news
people who distrust mainstream news tend to view influencers as more trustworthy and authentic than traditional media.

A report from Griffith University and Sentiment Agency, an Australian strategy agency, provides further evidence. 

It examined 564 political creator posts during the 2025 federal election. The findings show creators outpublished traditional media on election and leadership content by four to one on social media. Audiences also identified creators as particularly influential sources of political information. 

The research highlights that while traditional media may be seen by many as more credible, creators connect with audiences. This shapes what people pay attention to, rather than necessarily changing how they vote.

This strategy is not new

Research shows United States president Donald Trump’s media strategy helped him win the so-called first “influencer election” in 2024.

But his engagement with celebrities and content creators is not as simple as podcast appearances or algorithms. Instead, it reflects longstanding relationships with online communities, including those surrounding powerful celebrities such as Joe Rogan and Elon Musk. 

Political influence is more than borrowing a celebrity’s audience. It is about accessing the cultural relationships and credibility they have established. 

It doesn’t always result in election wins, though. The “Kamala is Brat” phenomenon – which emerged after singer Charli XCX called Kamala Harris “brat” following the release of her Brat album – shows how celebrities, memes and popular culture can make politicians more relevant to younger audiences.

It comes with risk

Political commentary can alienate existing audiences. People may enjoy someone’s comedy or television appearances without necessarily trusting their political judgement.

There are other grey areas too. As political commentary increasingly occurs outside traditional journalism, celebrities and creators do not operate under the same editorial expectations around accuracy, verification and balance. 

Ultimately, the greatest influence of these celebrities may not be changing individual votes. It is likely in shaping the conversations that precede them. They influence which issues dominate attention, how audiences perceive political leaders, and whose explanations they find credible.

In an increasingly fragmented media environment, that is actually a significant form of political power.
news.summary: Celebrities may not directly sway people’s votes but they do shape conversations in the media. That is a significant form of political power.

news.title: Sneaky troll polls boost the left  yet we keep falling for them
news.text:
Fake polls aren’t always fake news.

For the second time this year, a new pollster has been caught flat-out fabricating political survey data.

In August, Median Strategies was exposed as bogus after claiming its published poll showed that socialist Francesca Hong had a 23-point lead in the Democratic primary for governor of Wisconsin. She lost.

Now we learn that Wedgewood Polls, another new polling company that emerged this election cycle, was a complete fraud.

The company admits that just one of the 17 polls it published this year was real.

Only after the poll-analysis site FiftyPlusOne investigated and caught the fraud did Wedgewood claim that it was really running a prank or a sting.

It aimed, the “firm” said, to “test a simple hypothesis: How easy is it for an entirely fabricated polling firm to gain traction, be taken seriously, and expose how little scrutinization exists in media and public commentary?”

Good for FiftyPlusOne — but until then, the site had included Wedgewood’s polls in its election data.

So did The New York Times, Decision Desk HQ, Vote Hub, and the biggest name in the business, Nate Silver.

Wedgwood polls were cited on MS NOW and touted by Mississippi Democrat Scott Colom when its survey showed him tied in his US Senate race against Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.

The fake polls have shown good news for both Democratic and Republican candidates, and sometimes for establishment Democrats such as Karen Bass against progressive challengers.

But overall they’ve favored Democrats, and have specifically boosted the electability of Democratic Socialists.

Silver’s model became a bit more favorable to Republicans after he removed the fake polls from his calculations.

Liberal columnist Bill Scher raised the alarm months ago about pollsters with sketchy histories helping Graham Platner in Maine and Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan.

Now we’re hearing an I-told-you-so chorus from the camps of Haley Stevens and Mallory McMorrow, the two Democrats who lost to El-Sayed.

McMorrow had to drop out when plunging poll numbers — including a June Wedgewood poll that had her in single digits — cratered her fundraising.

On X, she blamed Wedgewood: “Donations dried up, volunteers were devastated and pleading for guidance on what to do,” and “Reporters hounded me with calls to drop out.”

A McMorrow SuperPAC fundraiser said the poll “was used by several donors to pull back funding at a time we were being outspent by $80 million.”

Neera Tanden, a vocal Stevens supporter, added: “Man the pollsters that showed Haley behind over the summer were either made up or highly partisan. And a lot of smart people fell for the op.”

Gary Peters, the outgoing Democratic incumbent, worried aloud during the primary that misleading polls were distorting the outcome.

As it turned out, El-Sayed won by a much narrower margin than the polling had projected.

The last big fake-polls scandal broke in 2010, when a firm called Research 2000 published bogus surveys for progressive blog Daily Kos — and founder Markos Moulitsas sued the company for fraud.

Then as now, R2k’s fake polls shaped political reality in Democratic primary contests by showing progressive candidates to be electable in the general election.

In hotly contested primaries, electability is often a big issue: Hard-edged or scandal-tarred candidates such as El-Sayed, Hong and Platner need to persuade voters that nominating them isn’t a recipe for defeat in the fall.

Their opponents want to send the opposite message — recall the objections Donald Trump and Bernie Sanders faced in 2016.

This creates demand from all corners for polls on the electability question.

Now, as prediction markets mean big money riding on poll data, fake polls find an even larger audience.

Despite the scandals, we shouldn’t just ignore the polls.

When read with a properly skeptical eye, they have a good track record of showing what is electorally likely or possible.

They’re never going to be an exact science — and sometimes, even good pollsters just get one wrong.

Ann Selzer of the Des Moines Register, the dean of Iowa polling, retired after a way-off late 2024 poll predicted a Kamala Harris victory in the Hawkeye State.

Trump won Iowa by 13 points, then sued Selzer for fraud.

It was a ridiculous lawsuit, and was rightly thrown out of court.

But publishing polls that were never taken at all? That’s fraud.

A simpler lesson is for voters and reporters alike to demand that pollsters have a track record before we trust them.

There are plenty of known names in the business, from the granddaddy of them all (Gallup) to newspaper and university polls.

Some have been proven reliable; others have a known bias — but at least you know what you’re getting.

A brand-new pollster with no track record, no known institution behind it, and nobody checking its work? Voter beware.

Dan McLaughlin is a senior writer at National Review. X: @BaseballCrank

news.text:
President Donald Trump fumed about basketball star LeBron James on Truth Social Thursday, accusing the athlete of disrespecting the nation by continuing his warm-up routine during a pregame performance of “The Star-Spangled Banner.”

In a post paired with a video of James swinging his arms and appearing to practice his shot ahead of his Tuesday night debut with the Philadelphia 76ers, Trump wrote, “While listening to our National Anthem, LeBron James disrespects our Country!”

“I said right from the beginning that he’s no good, a TOTAL DISGRACE,” the president said of James, someone he’s publicly clashed with in the past.

“LeBron James should apologize to all of those Great American Warriors and Heroes who died for the American Flag and all that our Country stands for!”

James and Trump have a history of trading insults. The NBA veteran, who campaigned for Democrat Hillary Clinton in 2016 and endorsed Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024, knocked the president’s reaction to Golden State Warriors star Steph Curry, saying he’d vote against visiting the White House if Trump invited the team to celebrate their 2017 championship.

“U bum,” James posted on X. “@StephenCurry30 already said he ain’t going! So therefore ain’t no invite. Going to White House was a great honor until you showed up!”

Trump sneered when asked whether he thought James or NBA legend Michael Jordan was the greatest basketball player of all time back in July, saying he thought James may be “racist” and that, “I only like people that like me.”

Trump sneered when asked whether he thought James or NBA legend Michael Jordan was the greatest basketball player of all time back in July, saying he thought James may be “racist” and that, “I only like people that like me.”
